sentence: I told my wife she was drawing her eyebrows too high. She looked surprised. I haven't seen her since, which is fair, because apparently that joke has been making the rounds since the Pleistocene. The eyebrows, however, remain at full mast wherever she is. They have a life of their own now. I just hope they're happy.

I used to hate facial hair. Then it grew on me. My beard, meanwhile, has filed a formal complaint about being made into a pun for the third time this month, and is currently considering legal representation by my moustache, who is very expensive and only handles cases involving handlebars.

A friend of mine claims he can communicate with vegetables. He says he speaks fluent cabbage, decent broccoli, and only kitchen-Spanish levels of leek. I asked him what the carrots had to say and he told me, with a completely straight face, that root vegetables are mostly into politics, and they are extremely opinionated about parsnips.

I bought some shoes from a drug dealer. I don't know what he laced them with, but I've been tripping all day. My doctor says it could be the laces or it could be the lack of cardio, and frankly neither of us is willing to commit to a diagnosis until the carpet finishes apologising for the bruises on my knees.

Time flies like an arrow. Fruit flies like a banana. Existential dread, in my experience, flies first class on someone else's air miles and has a meltdown about the legroom. The whole metaphor falls apart if you think about it for more than seven seconds, but then again so does most of my life, and I've made peace with it.

I'm reading a book about anti-gravity. It's impossible to put down. My partner is reading a book about glue. She says it's quite gripping. Between us we are basically operating a small pun-based reading group, and our library memberships will eventually be revoked for crimes against literature, which is something I will accept with dignity.

I went to a seafood disco last week. I pulled a mussel. Then I tried to lure a date with my best lines and got nothing but cold shoulders from the prawns, who, it turns out, are not into men with my level of shell-shocked stage presence. The bouncer told me kindly that maybe I should fish elsewhere.

My friend's bakery burned down last night. Now his business is toast. He says he kneads a new oven, but frankly the dough situation is half-baked at best, and he's been crusty about the whole thing ever since. I suggested he loaf around for a few days before deciding anything, and he kicked me out of the kitchen.

Why don't scientists trust atoms? Because they make up everything. I told this to my chemistry teacher, who closed her eyes for several seconds and then asked, very quietly, whether I'd considered a career in any field that doesn't involve speaking to other human beings. I am now studying mime, which she also seems to disapprove of.

I had a date with a calendar girl. It didn't last a year. To be fair, I'd been seeing her on and off since February, but our schedules never quite lined up, and by November she said she needed a fresh page. I'm now dating a watchmaker, which is also going badly but at least the breakups are very punctual.

Why is it that when you're running late, every single traffic light in the city has a personal grudge against you, but on a Sunday when you have nowhere to be, you sail through eleven greens in a row like the chosen one, and there's nobody in the passenger seat to be impressed? You can't even brag about it to anyone, because the only witness is a half-eaten croissant on the dashboard.

Supermarket self-checkout has become a strange kind of performance art where you stand under a spotlight, weighing your own onions while a robot voice accuses you of stealing. There is always an unexpected item in the bagging area, and the unexpected item is always your dignity. An attendant comes over and presses a button that I'm convinced does nothing, then walks away looking deeply tired.

There's a very specific kind of person who, when the lift arrives and the doors open, marches in before letting anyone else out. I would like to gently propose that we, as a society, push them down a small hill. Nothing serious. Just a respectful, well-padded hill, with a soft landing and a long mirror at the bottom so they can have a good hard look at themselves.

Adulthood is mostly being shocked by how often you have to buy bin bags. You think you've solved bin bags. You bought a roll three weeks ago, you have entered your bin-bag era. Then there are no bin bags. There have never been any bin bags. The roll has vanished into the same dimension as all the missing socks, and you're back in the cleaning aisle, defeated.

When you're a child, you cry because you don't want to go to bed. When you're an adult, you sit on the edge of the sofa staring blankly into the middle distance until 1 a.m., resenting the fact that you have to walk approximately four metres to lie down. This is, I am told, called personal growth. It does not feel like growth.

Airport security is the only place on earth where a fully grown adult will voluntarily take off their belt and shoes in front of strangers and then put a half-empty bottle of water in a clear plastic bag as if presenting evidence. We do all of this without complaint, then complain bitterly about a four-minute queue at passport control because by then we have, as a culture, exhausted our patience for the day.

Whoever decided that fitted sheets should exist clearly never had to fold one. Mine is currently a sort of lopsided cotton orb that lives at the back of the airing cupboard, judging the rest of the linen. Every time I open the door it falls out, looks at me, and rolls back in. I have considered moving house just to leave it behind.

The phrase 'I'll just be a minute' is the most popular lie in any household. It is on par with 'I'll start the diet on Monday' and 'I will read that book one day'. Together, they form the holy trinity of harmless domestic dishonesty, and they have brought more comfort to humanity than any organised religion currently in operation.

Why is it that the moment you decide to clean out the fridge, an item that has been quietly fermenting in the back for six months suddenly becomes radioactive? You open one container and three other lifeforms make themselves known. You shut the door. You go for a walk. You come back and pretend nothing happened. The fridge respects this contract.

The hardest part of any social gathering is the bit where everyone agrees the evening is over but nobody is willing to actually leave. We stand in the doorway with our coats half on, recapping the entire night for forty minutes, while the host's smile gets a little tighter and a little more architectural. Eventually somebody opens a second bottle out of pure desperation, and we are stuck for another hour.

I went to the gym for the first time in two years yesterday. The instructor asked what my goals were and I said, with what I thought was disarming honesty, 'survive this hour'. She did not laugh. She put me on something called the assault bike, which is named, I now realise, after what it does to your soul.

My life is a bit like a productivity app I downloaded with great enthusiasm three weeks ago. The notifications kept arriving until I muted them, then I forgot it existed, and now it just sits there on the second screen, slightly judgemental, never opened. To be honest, the parallels are getting uncomfortably specific, and I might need to delete the app.

Every time I cook something ambitious I tell myself this is the meal that will turn me into a person who hosts dinner parties. So far it has produced a small kitchen fire, a casserole that even my dog refused, and one extremely successful soup that I have now made twelve weeks in a row. I am, in essence, a one-soup man, and the soup is barely a soup.

I'm at the age now where I bend down to pick something up, and my body holds a brief meeting before deciding whether to come back upright. Sometimes the vote goes against me, and I have to live my life from the floor for a while, which has been surprisingly fine. The floor is honest. The floor doesn't expect anything from you. We have an understanding.

I told my therapist I have abandonment issues, and she said our session was up. I'm joking. She would never. She would, however, gently note that I just defused a serious feeling with a punchline for the fourth time this hour, and would I like to sit with the discomfort instead. I would not. I never would. That's why she costs what she costs.

I have the kind of memory that can recall every embarrassing thing I did between the ages of eleven and twenty-two with crystal clarity at three in the morning, but cannot retain the PIN of the card I have owned for six years. The mind is a remarkable instrument, in the sense that mine is a kazoo and somebody else has the orchestra.

I tried to learn the guitar during lockdown, like everyone else. Five years later, I can play a strangled approximation of Wonderwall, and that's it. My neighbours have offered, very politely, to buy the guitar from me at any price. I have declined, because the guitar and I are working through some things together, and a sale would feel like abandonment.

I went on a first date last week and tried to be mysterious. Apparently the trick to being mysterious is to talk less than you would normally talk. I had no idea this rule existed and discussed my dental anxieties for forty-five minutes before realising she had been silently nodding for what I now suspect was sport. There will not be a second date.

My doctor told me I needed to do more cardio. I told my doctor I was very busy. My doctor said she didn't realise I was so important. I told her I have a queue of admin tasks waiting for me at home that I am also avoiding, and that the only exercise I get is moving things around mentally to feel better about not doing them. She wrote 'consider therapy' on the chart.

I've been told I have a face that's good for radio, and that my voice is excellent for podcasts you don't listen to. Honestly, I'll take it. Two compliments wrapped in cling film and presented to me with a small bow on top. I framed the first one. The second one I keep in the drawer with the spare batteries, for when I need to feel humbled.

I was at the post office yesterday when a pigeon walked in, took a ticket, and waited patiently in the queue. Nobody acknowledged this. When its number was called, it stepped up to the counter, presented a small parcel, paid in seeds, and left through the automatic doors without making eye contact. We all carried on as if this was completely normal, because in Britain, that's what you do.

My fridge has started leaving me little notes. Yesterday's said 'You are not the person I thought you were'. I don't know what I did to upset it. I bought it nice yoghurts. I keep the temperature consistent. I think it might be having a midlife crisis, which would be its first life and only crisis, so I should probably be more patient with it than I have been.

A man in a chicken costume tried to recruit me into a pyramid scheme outside the train station this morning. I told him I was already in three. He looked devastated, removed his beak, and asked if I could put in a good word with my upline. I cannot. My upline is a man named Greg who once tried to sell me a timeshare in a boat, and we are no longer on speaking terms.

The moon called. It said it was tired of being a satellite and wanted to try something new. I suggested freelance graphic design, and it told me it had no hands. We sat with that in silence for a while. Eventually I offered to be its career coach for a modest fee, and it agreed, on the condition that all our meetings happen at night.

My therapist asked me to draw a picture of how I was feeling. I drew a small horse on fire. She asked what the horse represented. I said the horse was the horse. She asked what the fire represented. I said it was on fire. We have been going around in this circle for about forty minutes and I think we may have stumbled onto something, although neither of us is sure what.

I have a sourdough starter named Geoffrey. Geoffrey demands attention twice a day, has strong opinions about which flour I use, and recently refused to rise unless I read to him from a particular biography of Disraeli. I am not making this up. Geoffrey is older than my niece and considerably more high-maintenance, and yet I love him in a way I cannot fully explain to my family.

I tried to return a vacuum cleaner last week and the shop assistant asked if it was faulty. I said no, but it had begun composing music. She nodded as if this was a known issue, took the vacuum, gave me a refund, and very quietly mentioned that the dishwashers had been doing the same thing. I left before she could say anything else, and I haven't been back since.

There's a fox who lives at the end of our street and I'm starting to suspect he runs the neighbourhood. He has nodded at me on three separate occasions. Last week I saw him sitting outside the chip shop as if waiting for somebody, and on Sunday he was making what I can only describe as eye contact with the corner shop owner through the window. Nothing about this man is normal.

I went to a job interview last Tuesday and was asked, in all seriousness, where I saw myself in five years. I said, 'Asleep. Hopefully somewhere quiet.' The room went still. The interviewer wrote something down very slowly. I did not get the job. I did, however, get a follow-up email asking if I'd be interested in a part-time role in their wellness initiative, which feels like a different kind of victory entirely.

Last night my microwave beeped at me thirty seconds before I set it to. I confronted it about this and the door fell open in what I can only describe as a sulk. We are now in a stand-off. I refuse to apologise first, and the microwave refuses to heat my soup. I will starve before I lose this, although the soup is starting to look quite reasonable cold.

sentence: Every meeting could have been an email, every email could have been a Slack message, and every Slack message could have been left unsent for the rest of human history with no measurable impact on the productivity of our species. And yet here we are, on a call about a call we had last Thursday, scheduling a follow-up call. The capitalism is calling from inside the house.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: IT support asked me if I'd tried turning it off and on again. I said yes. They asked if I had really tried turning it off and on again. I said yes. They came over, turned it off, turned it on again, and it worked. I asked them what they had done differently. They said, 'I believed in it.' That is, apparently, the entire degree.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: The printer is the only piece of office equipment that knows it is feared, and it uses that fear. It jams the morning before a big presentation. It runs out of magenta when nobody has used magenta in eleven months. It demands a software update at 4:55 on a Friday. The printer is not a machine. The printer is a feudal lord, and we are its peasants.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: I asked my smart speaker to set a timer for ten minutes. It played jazz from 1962. I asked it again. It ordered me a kilo of frozen prawns. I gave up and now eat my pasta whenever the prawns arrive, which is roughly every Tuesday. My life has improved measurably since I stopped trying to control the technology and started letting it parent me instead.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Schrödinger's cat is in a box and may be either alive or dead. My inbox is a box and definitely contains both an unread email from my manager and the will to live, in superposition. The act of opening either one will collapse the wavefunction in a way I am not emotionally prepared for. So I leave both unobserved, scientifically speaking, and the universe holds its breath.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Our company values, written in huge letters on the lobby wall, are Innovation, Integrity, and Impact. The first one means the coffee machine is broken. The second one means somebody stole my lunch and lied about it. The third one means we are now hiring a Chief Vibes Officer, whose job is to issue motivational quotes via the office Slack channel that nobody opens.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Two physicists walk into a bar. The first one says, 'I'll have a glass of H2O.' The second one says, 'I'll have a glass of H2O too.' The second physicist dies. This joke has been doing the rounds in physics departments for forty years, which tells you everything you need to know about the dating prospects of physicists.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: My code worked perfectly until I added a single semicolon, and now my computer is on fire. Stack Overflow tells me the issue was resolved in 2014. The accepted answer is, 'I figured it out, never mind,' with no further information. I have written a stern email to the user who posted this, who has not logged in since 2015 and may, statistically, no longer be alive.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: Evolution is, frankly, embarrassing. We had millions of years and ended up with a back that doesn't work, knees that file a complaint at thirty, and a tendency to invent religions about whichever animal looks scariest. The dolphins are doing fine without any of this. The dolphins do not have to file taxes. We need to have a serious conversation with whoever was in charge.

subtopic: humour about work, tech, or science
sentence: I left a sticky note on my monitor that says 'BACK IN 5 MINUTES'. That was eleven months ago. Nobody has questioned it. Two new hires have started, three people have left, and the note is now a load-bearing piece of office culture. If I take it down, I genuinely believe the ceiling will come with it. So it stays, and I keep meaning to come back.

There are 10 kinds of people in this world: those who understand binary, those who don't, and those who didn't realise this was a joke until somebody explained it to them at a party, ruining the joke and the party simultaneously. I have personally been all three of those people, sometimes within the same conversation.

My code has two states: working, and 'I haven't found the bug yet'. There is no third state. The 'finished' state is a myth promoted by project managers to keep developers compliant, much like the famed 'last sprint' before launch, which has historically been followed by between eleven and forty-seven additional 'last sprints' depending on the size of the company.

A SQL query walks into a bar, walks up to two tables, and asks: 'Mind if I join you?' Nobody at the bar laughed, which is fair, because the joke has been doing the rounds in database circles since the early 2000s, and at this point it's basically a primary key in the table of bad puns. I'm sorry. I'll see myself out.

I asked the AI to refactor my function and it added six new dependencies, deleted my tests, and renamed everything in German. The PR description was a sonnet. The senior engineer who reviewed it just typed 'no' and went home. I respect both of them, in different ways, for entirely different reasons, and I am still trying to undo the German.

Everything in software is named after either food or wizards. Kafka, Hadoop, Pickle, Cookie, Sandwich, Gandalf the Build System, Merlin the CI Pipeline, and a deployment tool called Frodo that nobody is willing to deprecate because the person who named it is now a vice president. The industry will collapse before we agree on naming conventions, and I respect that.

The bug was reported at 4:55 on a Friday. By 4:57, three engineers had pasted it into Slack with the words 'this is interesting'. By 5:02, it had been escalated to staff-level. By 5:15, somebody had filed a JIRA ticket and immediately gone home for the weekend, leaving the rest of us trapped in a meeting that nobody had agreed to be in.

There are two kinds of git commit messages: 'fix typo' and a sprawling six-paragraph essay that nobody will read. There is no middle ground. Anybody who claims to write tidy, descriptive commit messages either lied on their CV or has been doing exactly the same project for fourteen years and never has to onboard anyone new.

I tried turning it off and on again. I tried turning it off and on again twice. I tried unplugging it, blessing it, naming it after my dead grandmother, and reading it the changelog aloud. Nothing worked until a junior intern walked past and breathed near the cable. The cable, presumably, is now my new manager. I will be reporting to the cable from Monday.

Why do programmers prefer dark mode? Because light attracts bugs. I told this to my dentist, who, I now realise, is not a programmer, and has very limited patience for puns delivered at full volume with a mouth full of suction tube. She did not laugh. She did, however, drill deeper than I think was strictly necessary on the tooth in question.

I spent four hours debugging today, and the bug turned out to be a single missing comma. I have been a software engineer for nine years. I have a master's degree. My hourly rate could comfortably feed a small village. And today, my actual job was to find one comma. The senior engineer says this never gets less humbling. I believe him. I believe him deeply.

I don't trust stairs. They're always up to something. My wife rolled her eyes so hard yesterday I'm worried about her optic nerve. The kids have started leaving the room when they hear me clear my throat in a particular way, because they know exactly what's coming, and I don't blame them. I would also flee, if I weren't trapped in this body, telling these jokes, by genetic decree.

I made a pencil with two erasers once. It was pointless. My son physically left the country shortly after I told this joke at his graduation. I do not know where he is. I have, however, just thought of three more for his wedding, whenever that happens, and I will deliver them with full enthusiasm, ideally over a microphone, while wearing a slightly bad suit.

My daughter asked me to make her a sandwich, so I said 'Poof, you're a sandwich.' She is twenty-six years old and a successful lawyer, and she still walked out of the room. There is a special pride in being the kind of father whose love language has not evolved meaningfully since 1987. I wear it with dignity, mostly because nobody else is going to.

I told my kids a joke about pizza. It was too cheesy. I told them a joke about construction. I'm still working on it. I told them a joke about a calendar. Its days were numbered. They have started, very quietly, pricing up the cost of moving out, even though the youngest is nine. I consider this a sign of healthy ambition and good comedic taste.

Hello hungry, I'm Dad. I have been doing this since 1994, and I have never once had a child laugh genuinely at it. The performance, however, is not for them. The performance is for me, and for the long unbroken chain of fathers stretching back to the Pleistocene who said the equivalent of this joke and were also met with stony silence at the family fire.

What do you call a fish with no eyes? A fsh. My wife told me, very gently, that this joke does not work in writing, and frankly, it doesn't really work out loud either. I am still telling it. It is now a matter of principle. There are bad jokes I am willing to die on the hill for, and the fsh joke is, somehow, the one I have chosen for my legacy.

Why don't eggs tell jokes? They'd crack each other up. The kids have asked me, repeatedly, to retire this joke. The kids are not in charge of my repertoire. I have built up a portfolio of approximately seven hundred of these over the last two decades, and they will be hearing each of them at least twice more before I expire, plus a posthumous reading at the funeral. It's in the will.

I'm reading a book about teleportation. It's bound to take me places. I delivered this joke to a colleague at the office Christmas party, and he stared at me for a long time before saying, 'You're really doing this, aren't you?' I assured him I was. We have not spoken since. I assume he is busy. I assume his new role doesn't involve interacting with people who make book jokes.

I used to play piano by ear. Now I use my hands, like everyone else. I told this to my son's new girlfriend the first time she came over for dinner, and she gave me the kind of polite smile that suggested she was, in that moment, reconsidering several of her life choices. She has not been back. My son no longer makes eye contact with me at family gatherings.

Did you hear about the kidnapping at the playground? They woke him up. That joke is forty years old and so is my back. Both of them still mostly work, but they make a strange sound first thing in the morning, and I find myself defending them to younger generations who don't appreciate the craft involved in maintaining either. I will, regardless, continue.

Why did the chicken cross the road? Because, statistically, chickens move along the path of least resistance to food sources, and in this case, the corn was on the other side. That's it. That's the entire explanation. There is no punchline. I have ruined this joke for myself, and now I am going to ruin it for you too, because suffering is one of life's few truly equitable distributions.

A man walks into a bar. He orders a drink. He pays for it. He sits there for about forty minutes, finishes his beer, settles his tab, and goes home. He has a perfectly fine evening. The next morning, he goes to work. There is no twist. He is just a man who had a quiet drink. I find this joke restful. The world does not always need a punchline. Sometimes it needs a man and a beer.

What's the difference between a duck? One of its legs is both the same. That sentence has been broken by design, and I will not be repairing it. If you have a strong urge to fix the grammar, please direct that energy into something more useful, like writing a will, or finally calling your mother, both of which you have been putting off for entirely too long.

Knock knock. Who's there? Nobody. Just me. I am the one who knocked. I have been standing here for several minutes and I have lost the thread of why I came over in the first place. This is no longer a joke. This is what a midlife crisis sounds like on a Tuesday afternoon, and I would appreciate it if you would let me in, because it is unexpectedly cold and I forgot my coat.

How many surrealists does it take to change a lightbulb? A fish. That joke used to work. Then everyone heard it. Then everyone started doing it. Then the surrealist art community formally voted, in 1997, to retire the format. The bulb, of course, has not been changed. The room is dark. We are all sitting here making fish jokes in the gloom, which is, frankly, on-brand.

What did the fish say when it swam into a wall? Nothing. Fish do not have vocal cords in the way humans do, and even if they did, they would not waste them describing a banal collision to a passing colleague. Fish are dignified creatures with limited need for verbal complaint. We could learn from them. Mostly, we do not. We mostly just put them in lemon and butter.

Why was six afraid of seven? Because seven was a registered sex offender. That joke is the reason I am no longer allowed to give the speech at family weddings, and honestly, it's probably a fair call. I'm not sure what I expected. I just felt the room had become too cheerful, and I wanted to introduce some friction. I did. The friction is permanent. The friction is, in fact, the new room.

I told my friend a joke about UDP. I'm not sure if he got it. That joke depends on you understanding UDP, a network protocol famous for not confirming whether the message arrived. If you understood the joke, congratulations, you are a horrible person. If you didn't, please continue to live your life unburdened by this knowledge. It will serve you better than it has served me.

Two cannibals are eating a clown. One says to the other, 'Does this taste funny to you?' The other one says, 'Yes.' That's it. The straight answer is the joke. Comedians have spent decades constructing elaborate punchlines, and it turns out you can just say 'yes' to a setup and call it a day. The whole industry, frankly, has been overcomplicating things. Apologies to my former agent.

Why did the man drop his ice cream? Because he was hit by a bus. That's the joke. It is not a good joke. It does, however, illustrate a useful principle, which is that not all setups deserve a clever payoff, and not all suffering is meaningful. Sometimes a man just loses his ice cream, and the universe shrugs. The ice cream cone, for what it's worth, ended up on the pavement.

My toddler ate three crayons today and is now drawing inside herself, which I'm told is technically art. The pediatrician was unimpressed and gave me the kind of look that suggested she sees this exact scenario weekly. I asked if there was anything to worry about. She said only the cost of replacement crayons, which I considered, on reflection, to be a fair joke.

Before I had children, I had many opinions about how other people raised their children. I had carefully thought-through views on screen time, sugar, bedtimes, and tantrums in supermarkets. I now have one child, no opinions, and a Peppa Pig DVD I would willingly trade my driving licence for, just to get fifteen minutes of silence so I can drink a single hot cup of tea.

Bedtime in our house is a forty-five minute negotiation involving water, a story, another story, a different water, a toilet trip, a second toilet trip, an existential question about the universe, and finally a small piece of cheese. My five-year-old has the negotiating instincts of an international diplomat, and unless I bring my best game, the cheese always wins.

I now understand why my mother used to lock herself in the bathroom and pretend she couldn't hear us. I previously considered this behaviour deeply unfair. I now consider it the foundational survival skill of parenthood. I have my own bathroom now. I am in it more than I would like to admit. The Wi-Fi reaches in here, which is, frankly, the only home improvement I deeply care about.

Children are an excellent investment, if your goal is being interrupted approximately seven hundred times during the only good film you have rented in a year. I have watched the first ten minutes of every prestige drama released since 2019. I have not seen the middle of any of them. I do not know what happens. I will go to my grave unsure whether anyone in any of these series ever actually solved anything.

My son asked me where babies come from at the bus stop in front of twelve strangers. I gave him a vague, dignified answer involving love and hospitals. He then asked, very loudly, what an epidural was. I had a coughing fit. The bus arrived. I have never been so happy to see public transit in my entire life. We do not, in this house, discuss the rest of the journey.

I packed every conceivable item for a family day at the beach. Sun cream. Snacks. Spare clothes. A first aid kit. Towels. A novel I will not read. Three different hats. My daughter cried for fifty minutes because I forgot the one specific yellow bucket. The yellow bucket was at home. The yellow bucket is, somehow, the only bucket. I cannot explain why. I have never been forgiven.

My children have a sense of fairness that would impress a constitutional lawyer. Any perceived imbalance in the size of two biscuits is treated as a violation of human rights. I have, in the past, attempted to use a kitchen scale to settle disputes. The kitchen scale is now hidden because, according to my eight-year-old, it is biased against him. He has not provided evidence. The case continues.

The school sent home a paper requesting a costume for a class play. The notice arrived yesterday. The play is tomorrow. The costume specification is 'a Victorian chimney sweep'. I have given my son a black t-shirt, smudged him slightly with eyeliner, and handed him a small dustpan. If anybody asks, this is what Victorian children looked like. I refuse to take questions on the matter.

Sleep training, I have learned, is mostly the parents being trained. I am now able to fall asleep standing up, while gently rocking, holding a baby monitor in one hand and a half-finished sandwich in the other. My wife and I communicate in pre-language grunts. The baby sleeps eight hours a night. We sleep three. The baby is, by every measurable outcome, winning.

My profile says I enjoy hiking, but what I really enjoy is sitting on the sofa thinking about going hiking, which is a much more sustainable hobby and requires no actual hills. I match with people who have authentic photographs of themselves at the top of mountains, and then I have to invent reasons why my schedule never quite allows us to go to one together. The schedule, of course, is fine. The hills are the problem.

Every man on this app is either six foot four, owns a fish he is holding aloft like a trophy, or is currently 'between things'. I am not entirely sure what 'between things' means, but I suspect it covers a multitude of personal situations including bankruptcy, recent divorce, and a deep ongoing argument with his housemate. I have started swiping on the fish instead. The fish has more clarity of purpose.

His opening message was, 'Hey'. Just hey. No follow-up. Three days of silence followed. Then a second message: 'You up?' It was 9:43 in the morning. The man is asking me whether I am up, on a Tuesday, at almost ten in the morning. The whole conversation is a brilliantly compressed CV of every reason I should unmatch immediately, which I did, with a small fond smile.

We had a great first date. He paid for the drinks. He asked me questions. He laughed at the correct moments. I went home thinking, finally, a normal man. Three days later, he texted me a photograph of his foot. No context. No follow-up. Just the foot. I do not know what to do with this information. I am not equipped to process it. The foot remains in my camera roll like a strange digital ghost.

My friend told me to be more open-minded on dating apps. I followed her advice. I went on a date with a man whose hobbies included taxidermy and competitive whistling. He showed me a photograph of a stuffed badger he had named after his ex-girlfriend. I am, going forward, less open-minded. I have set strict new filters. The badger is, presumably, still in his living room, watching strangers come and go.

His profile said, 'Looking for my partner in crime'. I do not want to be anyone's partner in crime. I have a perfectly good day job and no appetite for federal charges. I would like to be someone's partner in doing the washing up, watching a film, and going to bed at a reasonable hour. The bar is somehow both higher and lower than it has ever been, and I cannot seem to clear it.

My bio currently says, 'I make excellent toast'. This is true. This is also, somehow, the only line about my personality I can write without dying inside a little. Every attempt at a witty self-summary makes me sound either desperately upbeat or like a hostage. The toast line has attracted exactly one match, a man with no photos, who messaged, 'What kind of toast?' I am marrying him next April.

Every man's first photo is him on a beach in Thailand. Every second photo is him with a sedated tiger. Every third photo is him at his best friend's wedding, which is the only photo where he looks like a normal person you could speak to. We need to acknowledge, as a culture, that the wedding photo is the only useful one. Everything else is performance. Just let me see how you look in a suit at someone else's event.

He arrived at the date forty minutes late, ordered the most expensive thing on the menu, talked exclusively about his startup, and asked me, at the end, whether I wanted to split the bill. I respect the boldness. I also got an Uber home, blocked his number, and have spent the past six months telling this story at parties, where it consistently earns a free drink from the listener. He has, in his own way, been a generous investment.

I matched with a man whose first sentence was a query about my five-year plan. I am thirty-four years old and I do not have a five-year plan. I have a vague, gently-held intention to eat more vegetables. That is the entire roadmap. I told him this. He thanked me for my honesty, unmatched me, and presumably went off in search of somebody with a properly-formatted PowerPoint about her future. I wish her well.

I bought a gym membership and went exactly once. The trainer asked what my goals were. I said, 'cardiovascular survival into my forties'. She laughed, which I found patronising, until I realised I was already winded just from walking to the rowing machine. The rowing machine has now seen more of me than my dentist has. I do not return its calls.

My yoga teacher keeps saying, 'find your edge'. I have found my edge. My edge is approximately twenty seconds into a downward dog, at which point my arms file a formal complaint with the rest of my body and I lie face-down on the mat pretending to be in a restorative pose. The instructor walks past, nods, and continues. We have an understanding now. The other students assume I am very advanced.

I told my personal trainer I wanted to look like a Greek statue. He said, 'Like the ones with missing arms and no clothes?' I said yes. He said, 'I can probably do the arms.' That is, in fairness, more accurate than I gave him credit for. Six months later I still have all four limbs, but I can now lift a small grocery bag without making a face. We are calling that a partial success.

The man on the treadmill next to me is running at what looks like roughly twenty-four kilometres per hour, while reading a hardback book, while drinking a coffee. I am walking at four, and the act of breathing through my nose is currently taking up most of my concentration. We are not the same species. I am attempting to make peace with that quietly, while pretending to adjust my headphones.

I have been doing the same beginner squats for six weeks and the only measurable change is that my legs hurt on more days of the week than they used to. The progress bar at the gym is, I am beginning to suspect, mostly imaginary. I am told this is normal. I am told it will pay off. I am also told to push through, which is currently being said to me by a person who clearly has not lived in my legs.

The gym always smells, faintly, like the regret of every January resolution that has ever been made and abandoned. The mirror is fluorescent in a way that flatters precisely nobody. The motivational poster on the wall says 'No Excuses!' in bright yellow, which is, frankly, the kind of slogan that makes me want to walk straight out, get a coffee, and reconsider the entire wellness industry from first principles.

I tried CrossFit once. The first thing I noticed was that nobody is allowed to call it CrossFit any more, due to a complicated legal dispute. The second thing I noticed was that the workout was named after a dead woman, which felt extreme. The third thing I noticed was that the man next to me was crying while doing burpees. I left during the warm-up. I have never looked back. The warm-up was the warm-up.

I went for a beginner's run. Two minutes in, my lungs filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of every internal organ. Four minutes in, my knees joined the suit as plaintiffs. Six minutes in, a small dog overtook me. The dog was on a lead. The lead was being held by a six-year-old. I made eye contact with the six-year-old. She gave me a thumbs up. I have not run since.

The personal trainer at my gym is twenty-three years old, has the body fat percentage of a particularly disciplined seabird, and refers to his clients as 'champ' in a tone that suggests he is unsure of all our names. He told me I had great potential, which is the polite trainer phrase for 'we are starting from the absolute bottom'. I will be billing him for the emotional honesty next week.

I joined a spin class because someone described it as 'fun'. There are many words for what spin class is. 'Fun' is not on the list. 'Wet'. 'Painful'. 'Loud'. 'Spiritually questionable'. 'Lit by the kind of disco lighting that suggests a 1990s nightclub robbery in progress'. I cycled vigorously in the dark for forty-five minutes while a stranger shouted at me about my potential, and then I went home and cried into a bowl of pasta.

The call centre put me on hold for an hour. When somebody finally answered, they said they were the wrong department and would have to transfer me. I was transferred. The hold music started again. After forty minutes, somebody picked up, said hello, and was immediately disconnected. I called back. The original hold queue restarted. I have, at this point, been on hold for the entire duration of a flight to Lisbon. I could have walked to Lisbon. I should have walked to Lisbon.

I phoned the council to query a bill. The automated system asked me to say, in plain English, what my problem was. I said, 'I would like to query a bill.' It said, 'I think you said: cancel my pet licence. Is that correct?' I do not have a pet licence. I do not know what one is. I shouted 'NO' at the phone for nine minutes, during which I was offered seven other unrelated services. I gave up and bought a goldfish instead. He is unlicensed and at peace.

The customer service representative apologised for the inconvenience seventeen times in the course of one phone call. I counted. By the eighth apology, I was apologising back, because the British in me cannot accept that much grovelling unilaterally. By the seventeenth, we were both apologising in stereo, the problem had not been addressed, and somebody in another country was probably timing this exchange for an efficiency report. I want a refund. I also want to send them a small gift.

The chatbot told me, with great enthusiasm, that my issue was extremely important and would be resolved shortly. It then asked me to rate my experience before I had explained the problem. I rated it one star and asked for a human. The chatbot told me, slightly hurt, that there were no humans available. I told it I did not believe in it any more. It logged me out. I have not slept properly since. The chatbot, somewhere, is winning.

I ordered a small bookshelf online. The website said delivery would take three to five working days. After ten working days I phoned the company. They said the bookshelf had been delivered. I said the bookshelf had not been delivered. They said, with confidence, that yes it had. To a different address. In a different city. They could not retrieve it. I now have a small bookshelf, somewhere in Hull, that has never met me and never will.

The receipt confirmation email arrived in my inbox before I had finished the transaction. It thanked me for my purchase of a single can of dog food, total cost forty-two pounds. I do not have a dog. The dog food was not in my basket. I phoned the supermarket. They told me the system was experiencing some difficulties and that I should treat any emails I received as 'aspirational'. I have framed this advice. I think about it every day.

I returned a faulty kettle to the shop. The assistant scanned it, looked at her screen, looked at the kettle, looked at me, and said with deep seriousness, 'This product does not exist.' I pointed at the kettle. She looked at it again. She said, 'No, this isn't a product we sell.' I produced the receipt. It bore her store's logo. She said, 'That's strange.' She put the kettle in a back room. I left without the kettle and without a refund. I will never know what happened next.

I was put through to a manager. The manager was indistinguishable from the previous person, only with a more apologetic tone and slightly slower diction. She offered me a ten percent voucher off my next purchase, which was generous, since I had already decided to never return to this company under any circumstances. I have framed the voucher. It is, I think, the closest thing to a personal apology I will ever receive in this lifetime.

The website asked me to confirm I was not a robot by selecting all the squares containing a traffic light. I selected them. It asked again. I selected them again. It told me I was wrong. There were no traffic lights in any of the squares the third time. I am, increasingly, beginning to suspect that the website itself is the robot, and I am the one being tested for compliance. I failed. The website will not let me purchase shoelaces.

I cancelled a subscription. They sent me a sad email. They sent me three more sad emails. They sent me a discount offer. They sent me a personalised plea from a member of the team. They sent me a survey about why I left. I did not answer. They sent me an apology for sending the survey, along with another survey. The cancellation, three weeks on, has still not gone through. I am, in their system, somehow more subscribed than I was before.

The man on the train opposite me has been making a phone call in a foghorn voice for forty-three minutes. He has discussed his dental work, his mother's opinions on his wife, and the precise terms of a contract he is renegotiating. I now know more about his life than I know about most of my own relatives. He has not lowered his voice. We have made eye contact twice. He winked the second time. I may have a new uncle.

Replacement bus services exist for the sole purpose of teaching the British public the meaning of true suffering. You wait at a station, in the cold, for forty minutes longer than the bus's stated arrival time. The bus, when it arrives, is the wrong size. The driver doesn't know the route. The route is somehow twice as long as the train. The whole experience is a small national curriculum in patience, delivered by the rail operator at no extra charge.

Somebody has eaten a tuna sandwich on the carriage and the smell has decided to stay for the rest of the journey. We are all pretending not to notice. The British capacity for silent collective suffering is being tested at peak strength. Nobody has moved. Nobody has opened a window. The tuna has won. We are now its passengers, and we will arrive at our destinations forever slightly damp with its memory.

The escalator at the station has been broken for so long that there is now a small plaque next to it acknowledging the loss. People walk up the dead escalator as though it were a war memorial. We mourn what it once was. I have a memory of riding it as a child, full of awe. Now we trudge. The station is not the same. The station will never be the same. The plaque is also broken.

The Tannoy on the platform announced, in cheerful tones, that the next train would be the 8:14 to Hove, calling at every station between here and the end of human patience. I was waiting for the 8:11 to London. I checked the board. The 8:11 was, according to the board, on time. The 8:11 did not exist. It had never existed. I had imagined the entire train. I went home. I am working from the kitchen table. I am writing this from the kitchen table.

On the bus, the woman next to me is talking to her plant. She is reassuring it that the journey will be over soon and that it will love the new flat. The plant, naturally, is not responding, but the woman is fluent in plant-conversation and is filling in both sides graciously. I am not eavesdropping. I am attending. They are having a much more meaningful exchange than I will all week, and I am here for it.

Why is the empty seat on the train always next to either the man who has fallen asleep with his mouth open or the very enthusiastic American backpacker who would like to know if you are familiar with the works of Kerouac. There is never an empty seat next to a quiet person reading a book and minding their business. The transit gods do not allow this. The transit gods are agents of chaos.

The tube was so packed this morning that I formed a brief romantic bond with a stranger's elbow. We have a shared history now. I do not know her name. She does not know mine. Her elbow and my left side, however, are now bound by a wordless understanding that will outlast most modern marriages. I disembarked at Embankment. The elbow continued onwards. I miss it sometimes.

The bus driver announced that the bus was no longer the bus. It was now, he said, terminating early due to operational reasons. We all looked at each other, unsure what to do with this information. One man asked, very reasonably, where the bus was now going. The driver said, 'home'. Then he turned the engine off. Then he turned the lights off. We were instructed to leave by the front door of a vehicle that had ceased to be a vehicle.

Every train announcement begins with 'We are sorry to announce' and ends with 'thank you for your patience'. The middle of the sentence varies, but the bookends do not. Together they form a perfect compressed metaphor for the entire British experience: apology, problem, apology, expectation that you will absorb the inconvenience without complaint. I have come to find it strangely comforting, in the way one might find a familiar local weather pattern comforting. It rains. The 7:42 is cancelled. Life goes on.

I have started a sourdough starter. It is now called Brian. Brian is more demanding than my last three relationships combined. Brian needs feeding twice a day. Brian sulks if the kitchen drops below twenty-two degrees. Brian has been with me longer than my current job. The bread Brian produces is, admittedly, excellent. But the emotional cost is substantial, and I am beginning to suspect that Brian is, in some quiet way, the head of the household.

Why do recipes always say 'one onion, finely chopped' as if this is a casual ask. It takes me forty minutes and three tea breaks to finely chop a single onion. By the end, I am crying, the cat has fled the room, and the onion is approximately the same level of chopped-ness as when I started. Cookbooks need to be honest about this. I would like a small chapter at the start called 'how long this will actually take', written in tears.

I made a curry from scratch last weekend. I bought twelve different spices. I toasted them. I ground them. I sweated onions for forty minutes. I followed a recipe by a chef whose face was on the cover of three different food magazines. The final dish tasted, identifiably, like the takeaway curry from the place around the corner. The takeaway curry costs nine pounds. The takeaway curry takes twenty minutes. I have learned an expensive lesson.

Avocados spend their entire lives in a perfect two-minute window between rock-solid and brown mush. There is no negotiation. There is no middle state. You check it on Tuesday: not ripe. You check it on Wednesday morning: not ripe. You check it on Wednesday afternoon: too late. The avocado has moved on without you. Each one is a small private exercise in mourning a vegetable's prime, and I am tired.

I attempted to make a soufflé. The internet promised me it was achievable for a competent home cook. I am, allegedly, a competent home cook. The soufflé rose magnificently for approximately ninety seconds, after which it collapsed in front of an audience of six guests at a dinner party. The soufflé made a small wheezing sound on its way down. I have not made another soufflé. I do not intend to. The episode is closed.

Microwave meal packaging is the only thing that lies to me with such consistency that I have come to rely on it. The picture on the front shows a generously plated dish, three large prawns, an arrangement of fresh herbs, and a sun-drenched lemon wedge. The actual contents, post-microwave, are a small grey paste, one prawn approximately the size of a fingernail, and a deep philosophical resignation about modern food production.

I went to a restaurant where the menu was twelve words long and the cheapest dish cost forty-six pounds. The waiter described each dish like a sommelier presenting a vintage. The plates arrived. They were the size of coasters. There was one carrot. The carrot had been deconstructed. I ate the carrot in two bites. I left still hungry, three hours older, and significantly poorer. I would, in fairness, go again. The carrot was, I admit, transcendent.

There is a banana on my kitchen counter that has been there for nine days. It is no longer recognisable as a banana. It is, at this point, an abstract sculpture about the passage of time. I do not have the courage to dispose of it. It deserves a small ceremony. I am planning to invite friends. There will be a reading. The banana will be honoured for its service before being committed to the compost bin.

Every weekend I tell myself I am going to do meal prep. Every weekend I buy the containers. Every weekend I buy the vegetables. Every Sunday evening, I order a pizza, look at the containers and the vegetables, feel a small private shame, and put the containers away clean. The vegetables remain in the fridge for six days before becoming a different, sadder set of vegetables, which I then also do not cook.

I asked the waiter if the dish was very spicy. He said, 'not at all'. He brought me a dish that has, technically, set my mouth on fire. I am still eating it. I am crying. I am sweating. I am ordering more bread. This is, as far as I can tell, my hill to die on. The waiter has not returned to the table, possibly out of pity, possibly because the kitchen has bet on whether I will finish, and they do not want to influence the outcome.

My cat has decided that the most comfortable place in the house is the keyboard of my laptop while I am trying to file my tax return. He has now contributed a number of his own characters to the document, and HMRC may, very shortly, receive a tax return that includes the sequence 'aaaaaaaaaalkjsd;;;;;;;;'. I am not removing it. I want to see what happens. We are in this together now.

My dog has, after seven years of patient training, learned exactly one trick: he sits when I say 'sit'. He does this with the grim resignation of a man finally cooperating with the police. He sits for approximately one and a half seconds. He then stands up again, as if to say, 'I did the thing. The thing has been done. We are not, however, friends now.' The trick book remains, I would say, ninety percent unfulfilled.

My rabbit, whose hobbies include chewing through cables and sulking, has destroyed three router power supplies this year. The cost of replacing them now exceeds the cost of the rabbit. We have an arrangement. He damages property. I sigh and order replacements. The internet is intermittently available. The rabbit, who pays no rent, lives like a small fur-covered medieval lord, redistributing the household budget by force.

I bought my cat a hundred-pound climbing tower with carpeted ledges, scratch posts, a hammock, and a small viewing platform. He has slept exclusively in the cardboard box it came in for six weeks. The tower remains unused. The box has been moved three times by my partner, in a futile attempt to convince the cat that the box is, in fact, the inferior product. The cat is unmoved. The box is now permanent furniture.

Dogs greet you as if you have just returned from a six-month deployment, even if you have only been to the bin. Cats greet you as if you have just walked into a private members' club where they are the senior partner and you have neglected to sign in. Both responses are objectively unreasonable. Both responses are also exactly why we have them, and the day they stop is the day I will know something is wrong.

I took my dog to a behavioural specialist because she had developed a habit of barking at the toaster. The specialist asked thoughtful questions, took notes, observed her for forty minutes, and concluded that my dog hated the toaster. The fee was a hundred and twenty pounds. I could, I think, have arrived at this diagnosis through quiet personal reflection. The dog and the toaster remain locked in their cold war. The toaster has not yet retaliated.

My hamster, Reginald, has a wheel. The wheel makes a noise that can be most accurately described as 'a small unoiled door, opened repeatedly, at three in the morning'. I have oiled the wheel. I have replaced the wheel. Reginald, somehow, always finds a wheel that squeaks. I have begun to suspect that Reginald is choosing the squeak deliberately, as a form of nonverbal complaint about something I cannot identify. I have accepted this. I have not slept properly in two years.

I have two cats. They are siblings. They have been together since birth. I cannot tell them apart visually, but I have learned to identify them by personality. One is a small terrorist with the manners of a Victorian aristocrat. The other is a gentle, slightly anxious creature who flinches when wind blows through the letterbox. They are, somehow, both incorrect responses to the world, and yet I love them more than I love most of my colleagues.

My dog has, despite hours of training, retained the worst possible recall in canine history. When I shout her name in the park, she looks at me with the polite curiosity of a stranger overhearing a private phone call, and then continues whatever she was doing. I have started to suspect she thinks her name is, in fact, a kind of distant weather phenomenon. Other people's dogs come when called. My dog interprets the call as informational at best.

The cat brought a mouse into the kitchen last night and laid it on the floor with great pride, as a gift. The mouse, on inspection, was very much alive. The mouse fled under the dishwasher. The cat, having delivered the gift, walked off to bed, considering her job done. The mouse and I have now been cohabiting for three days. The cat does not see this as her problem any more. The cat has, in a sense, retired.

I waved at someone across the street thinking it was an old friend. It was not an old friend. It was a stranger. The stranger waved back, looking confused. I committed to the bit. I crossed the road. We had a brief, polite conversation about nothing. I asked after his family. He has a family. I shook his hand. I am not sure he ever realised I did not know him. We exchanged numbers. I am terrified of what happens next.

Someone said, 'enjoy your meal,' and I said, 'you too.' The waiter does not need to enjoy my meal. The waiter is not eating my meal. The waiter has, in fact, eaten his own meal hours ago. He looked at me with the gentle pity of a man who has heard this before. I considered correcting myself. I did not. I committed to the social error and ate my entire dinner in shame. I have, to this day, never returned to that restaurant.

I went in for a handshake. He went in for a hug. We met somewhere in the middle in a kind of partial collision involving an elbow to my chest, a half-pat on my shoulder, and a confused noise I am not sure either of us has heard our own throats produce before. We are now colleagues. We see each other every Wednesday. We do not greet each other any more. We just nod, professionally, like two combat veterans who have agreed never to discuss the incident.

I forgot my colleague's name in the middle of introducing her to my husband. I stood there, smiling, mouth open, trying to summon a name I have known for three years. The silence stretched. Eventually I said, 'this is, of course, herself,' and gestured vaguely. My husband, to his credit, played along and shook her hand without commenting. She knew. She knows. We have never spoken of it. We never will. The friendship has survived on this unspoken contract.

I tried to be polite and held the door open for someone. They were further away than I thought. I waited. They walked slowly. I had committed. They walked more slowly. We made eye contact. There was no going back. They eventually arrived, ten seconds later than would have been comfortable, said 'thanks' with the energy of someone defusing a small bomb, and we both pretended that the door interaction had been perfectly normal. We were both wrong.

I went to a friend's birthday party and forgot to bring a card. I improvised by writing a heartfelt message on a paper napkin, which I then folded carefully and slipped into the gift bag. He found it. He read it in front of everyone. He cried. I had, in three minutes, written what was apparently the most meaningful thing anyone had ever given him. He brings it up at every gathering. I have, at this point, retired from card-giving altogether. The bar is too high.

I farted in a lift. There were two other people in the lift. We had eleven floors to go. Nobody moved. Nobody spoke. The doors took an entire geological epoch to open at each stop. I have moved cities since. I check the lift now before getting in, regardless of which building I am visiting. I cannot rule out that they have done the same. We are connected, the three of us, forever, by a brief atmospheric disturbance on a Tuesday afternoon.

My friend asked me what I thought of her new haircut. The haircut was, objectively, a disaster. I said, 'It's so brave.' She said, 'Brave?' I said, 'Yes, in the sense of bold.' She said, 'Bold?' I said, 'Yes, in the sense that it's a real statement.' She narrowed her eyes. I escaped by suddenly remembering an appointment. We have not discussed hair since. We will never discuss hair again.

I was on a video call and forgot I was on camera. I scratched my nose in a manner that, in retrospect, was significantly more involved than the social contract permits. Six colleagues watched. Nobody mentioned it. The meeting continued as if nothing had happened. I have, since, double-checked the mute and camera buttons approximately a thousand times before each call. I cannot, however, retroactively undo what was seen. Somewhere, in six different memories, the moment lives on.

I congratulated a woman on her pregnancy. She was not pregnant. The next twelve seconds were the longest twelve seconds of my adult life. She said, very kindly, 'I'm not, but thank you for noticing my new top, which is admittedly quite voluminous.' The grace with which she handled it has haunted me for years. I would not have been so generous. I would have buried me in the garden. She, however, sent me a Christmas card the following December. I am unworthy of her, and I know it.

Every Sunday afternoon, I stand in the front garden surveying my lawn with the gravity of a Roman general inspecting his troops. The lawn is, objectively, the same lawn as last week. I have, however, identified at least four new tactical problems with it. The neighbours pretend not to notice. The neighbours have also been doing this for years. We are all, collectively, holding the suburb together by the strength of our deep, unwarranted seriousness about grass.

I have begun referring to the loft as 'the loft' with the same reverence other men reserve for shrines. Up there, I have accumulated approximately fourteen years' worth of items I 'might need one day'. The items include a single ski boot, a working VCR, my wife's wedding dress, and a box labelled 'wires' that has been there since before our children were born. I am not allowed to throw any of it away. I am also not allowed to go up there alone, due to an unrelated incident in 2018.

I bought a barbecue four years ago. I have not allowed anyone else to operate the barbecue in that time. The barbecue and I have developed a sacred ritual involving the exact application of charcoal, the temperature of the coals, and a small set of muttered incantations. The food itself is, in fairness, almost always undercooked or charred, but the ceremony is the point. The ceremony is, in many ways, the entire culture of fatherhood compressed into one outdoor appliance.

The neighbour and I have had the same conversation, every Saturday morning, over the fence, for nineteen years. We discuss the weather, the state of the council, and the changes at the local pub. Neither of us says anything new. Neither of us wants to. Neither of us, I suspect, knows the other's middle name. We are, however, in deep, abiding friendship, by every metric that matters in this neighbourhood, and I would lend him my drill without hesitation.

I now own seven different jackets, none of which are appropriate for any specific kind of weather. There is the jacket for slightly damp Saturdays. There is the jacket for mowing. There is the jacket for the school run that I wear over the pyjamas, hoping nobody will notice. There is the jacket I bought because it had a small pocket for a phone, despite already owning four other jackets with phone pockets. My wife has, gently, suggested a wardrobe audit. I have, gently, refused.

The bird feeder in our garden has become the centre of an avian political drama I have grown emotionally involved in. There is a magpie who is bullying the smaller birds. There is a robin who has somehow, against all biological evidence, become the moral conscience of the operation. There is a squirrel who isn't, technically, allowed at the feeder, but who has been clearing it out at dawn for months. I have written to the manufacturer about the squirrel issue. I am pursuing the matter.

I have developed strong opinions about hose attachments. The ratcheting connector is, in my view, superior to the snap-on connector, although the snap-on is more convenient for the casual user. I have, in the past, attempted to share these views at dinner parties. My wife now squeezes my knee, gently, under the table, when I begin. The signal is unmistakable. I have, on occasion, ignored it. The dinner parties have, occasionally, suffered as a result.

Every weekend I tell my wife I am going to spend the morning in the shed. Every weekend I do, in fact, go into the shed. What I do in the shed is unclear, even to me. I move things around. I look at the toolbox. I consider rearranging the toolbox. I have one cup of cold tea. I emerge two hours later having achieved nothing measurable, but feeling deeply satisfied, as though something important has happened. The shed knows. The shed will not tell.

I have, over the years, developed what my wife calls 'the dad nap'. It can occur on any sofa, in any chair, at any hour after 2 p.m. on a weekend. It requires no announcement. It is brief, dignified, and, by all accounts, audible from the next room. The dad nap is the final form of paternal energy storage, and I have come into mine fully. The grandchildren will not see it. They will only see the man who emerges from it, suddenly alert, asking who took the last biscuit.

I bought a power washer. The power washer has changed me. I now look at every paved surface in the neighbourhood with the assessing eye of a man who knows what lies beneath the grime. I have power-washed the driveway, the patio, the side path, and, briefly, last Saturday, a small section of the neighbour's fence, without permission, before he came out and politely asked me to stop. I have not made a friend so much as a wary co-existence partner. I would still help him with his bins.

I retired six months ago, full of plans. I was going to learn Italian, write a memoir, finally get round to the loft. So far, I have learned six Italian words, written approximately one sentence of memoir, and spent eleven hours watching a documentary about narrow-gauge railways in mid-Wales. The retirement is, in many ways, working exactly as intended. I just had different intentions when I started.

I went for my routine eye test and the optician informed me, with great cheerfulness, that I have entered the stage of life where reading glasses are non-negotiable. I asked what stage that was. She said, 'middle age, sir.' I have not had time to process this. I am sixty-one years old. Middle age was supposed to be over by now. I am, apparently, still in it. Possibly forever. The optician has changed my plans entirely.

I now make a small involuntary noise every time I sit down on a low chair. The noise is somewhere between a sigh, a grunt, and a quiet philosophical complaint. My grandchildren have learned to imitate it. They do it now whenever they themselves sit down, in solidarity, even though they are eight and four respectively, and physically should not need to. The noise has become a family inheritance. I take a strange comfort in this.

I went to a concert last month. The bands were loud. The crowd was young. I left at 9:45. The concert started at 9:30. My wife and I agreed, on the way home, that this was unacceptable behaviour from the venue, who should have known to schedule the gig at a more sensible hour, say, around four in the afternoon, with a sit-down option. I have written to the venue. They have not, as yet, replied. I am drafting a follow-up.

I now require approximately ninety minutes of mental preparation to drive in the dark. I have to check the route. I have to consider the weather. I have to confirm that the destination is open. I have to inspect my reading glasses. I have to bring a flask. I have to inform somebody of my route, in case of incident. I have to consider whether the journey could be postponed until the morning. The journey, in question, is to the local Tesco, three miles away.

I joined a gentle yoga class for over-sixties. The instructor said we would start with 'easy stretches'. The first stretch involved reaching towards my toes. I have not seen my toes for some years, and we did not, on that occasion, achieve a reunion. The instructor told me to listen to my body. My body, very clearly, told me to lie down and have a small biscuit. I followed the instructions exactly. I was, by some margin, the best student.

The phrase 'in my day' has, against my own intentions, started slipping into my conversations with increasing frequency. I have caught myself complaining about pop music, the price of stamps, and the fact that nobody knows how to write a proper letter any more. I am, by every available metric, becoming my own father. The transformation is irreversible. My wife finds this both charming and alarming, often within the same sentence.

I went to bed at 8:45 on a Friday night, and I felt no shame. I felt, in fact, mild pride. The young people I used to know would be appalled. I would have been appalled, twenty years ago, by myself. I no longer recognise the man who used to go to the pub on Fridays. I do not miss him. He is, frankly, exhausted, and probably also already asleep, somewhere, with his shoes still on.

My grandson tried to show me how to use a new app on my phone. He moved his thumb at a speed that, frankly, was not legally permitted for use on a screen. I asked him to slow down. He slowed down by approximately twelve percent. Three minutes later, I no longer recognised the home screen. I do not know what app I am now in. He has gone home. I am stuck. My phone is, in some sense, no longer mine.

I bought a new mattress at the weekend. I spent forty-three minutes in the shop pressing different mattresses with the back of my hand, asking detailed questions about support and firmness, and quietly comparing return policies. I have become the kind of man who has strong views on lumbar alignment. Younger me would not have recognised this person. Younger me, however, did not sleep, and frankly, that man was not winning at anything.

I assembled a wardrobe over the weekend. Eleven hours of my life are gone. The wardrobe stands. It is, technically, a wardrobe. There is, however, one shelf that goes diagonally for reasons I cannot explain. There are also four screws I do not know what to do with. The instructions, in twelve languages, do not mention these screws. My wife says, 'we are leaving the screws in the kitchen drawer for now.' We are leaving the screws in the kitchen drawer forever.

I attempted to put up a shelf. I drilled into the wall, and the drill went straight through into the room next door. The room next door is my office. There is now a hole in my office wall, from which a small amount of plaster occasionally falls when somebody walks past upstairs. I have covered the hole with a small framed picture of a beach. The shelf, ironically, does not go on this wall. The shelf is still on the floor. The picture has, in fact, been more useful.

I decided to repaint the bathroom. The internet said it was a weekend job. The internet lied. Three weekends in, the ceiling is half-finished, the tiles are masked off, and the dust has spread into rooms that are not connected to the bathroom in any way I can explain. My wife has stopped asking when it will be done. She has, however, started saying, 'remember when we used a bathroom?' in a slightly wistful tone, which I am choosing to ignore.

I tried to fix the dripping tap. The internet told me it was a simple matter of replacing the washer. I bought eleven different washers, in case. I dismantled the tap. Water sprayed, in a great fountain, directly upwards into the ceiling. I learned, in that moment, that there is a separate water shut-off valve I should have used first. I have now learned this twice. I do not, evidently, retain plumbing lessons. The tap still drips. The ceiling now has a small stain.

I attempted to install a smart doorbell. The smart doorbell is now connected to my neighbour's Wi-Fi. The neighbour and I have not discussed this. The neighbour is getting notifications every time my postman approaches my house. I have decided to leave it as it is. The neighbour, by all evidence, finds it charming. He has begun sending me brief reports of my own deliveries. I will not be returning the smart doorbell.

I bought a saw. I used the saw exactly once. I now own a fence section that is slightly the wrong size, a piece of wood I do not know what to do with, and a small cut on my thumb that has, in the intervening months, achieved iconic status in family folklore. The saw lives in the shed. I am not allowed to touch it again without supervision. I do not contest this. The supervision is, frankly, reassuring.

I took the radiator off the wall to repaint behind it. I did not, at the time, fully appreciate the relationship between a radiator and the central heating system. I do now. The carpet had to be replaced. The plumber laughed for a full minute before quoting. He kept his card. He calls me, occasionally, just to check in. I think we have a friendship now, or possibly a long-term financial arrangement, and I am, frankly, not in a position to know the difference.

I painted the kitchen wall with what the chart described as 'a delicate dove white'. The wall is, in person, a haunting greyish-pink that has been described variously by visitors as 'bandage', 'gum', and 'a colour I associate with hospitals'. My wife has not commented. She is waiting, I think, for me to admit the failure unprompted. I will not. The wall, like the relationship, is allowed to have a difficult patch.

The light fitting in the hallway has been hanging at a slight angle for two years. I told my wife I would fix it. I told her this in March 2023. I am still going to fix it. The angle has, if anything, slightly increased. Visitors have started to comment. I have started to claim it is a feature, a deliberate 'asymmetric statement piece'. Nobody believes me. I do not believe me. The light fitting and I have entered into a quiet, mutual surrender.

I bought a flat-pack desk that promised assembly in 'under an hour'. Four and a half hours later, with three of the wrong screws in the wrong holes, I emerged victorious. The desk wobbles slightly when I lean on it. The drawer opens only at certain temperatures. It is, by any reasonable definition, a desk, and I refuse to acknowledge any of the more uncomfortable facts about it. We are working with what we have. The desk and I have an understanding.

Every family holiday begins with a vow that this one will be different, this one will be relaxing. Every family holiday ends, on day three, with my mother and sister having a polite, deeply venomous disagreement about a casserole, my father pretending not to hear it from the garden, and the children quietly forming a coalition to extract more ice cream from the situation. The vow has never, in forty years, been kept.

We rented a cottage in Cornwall for a week. The cottage had eight beds, two showers, and one tiny kitchen, and we crammed eleven adults and four children into it. By day four, three couples were quietly considering separation, my brother-in-law had taken to drinking his coffee at the bus stop just to be alone, and the four-year-old had bitten the eight-year-old over a Lego dispute. We have already booked it again for next summer. We learn nothing.

The car was packed at six in the morning. By 7:45 we had unpacked the car twice to look for a passport that turned out to be in my mother's coat pocket all along. We left at 9:13, an hour and a half behind schedule, with everyone slightly furious at each other and the youngest child crying because somebody had said the wrong word, very quietly, two miles back. The holiday had begun. We were already exhausted.

My father insists, every year, that he does not need a map. My father has, every year, ended up at a roundabout he does not recognise, in a town we did not intend to visit, while my mother quietly says, 'I told you to take the third exit, John.' He never takes the third exit. He has never, in fifty-three years of marriage, taken the third exit. The third exit is, by now, a metaphor for everything.

We went to a museum because somebody said it was educational. The children spent twenty-four minutes inside before requesting, in unison, that we leave. We had paid forty-eight pounds for the tickets. We had driven ninety minutes to get there. We left. We went to a service station. The children had ice cream. They speak fondly of the museum trip. They cannot, however, recall a single exhibit. They believe the museum was, fundamentally, an ice cream destination.

We attempted a family beach day. The wind was force seven. The sand was, by physical force, relocating itself into every crease of every sandwich. The youngest cried because a seagull made eye contact with him. The eldest demanded to leave because she was, quote, 'experiencing the worst day of her entire life'. We stayed for another forty minutes out of pure stubbornness. The photographs from that day will, one day, be treasured. They are, currently, evidence.

My aunt brought her own teabags. She brought, also, her own sugar, her own milk, her own kettle, and a small chair she prefers to sit in. She arrived at our holiday cottage and, within ten minutes, had reorganised the kitchen to her specifications. The rest of us pretended not to notice. We tried to make our own tea. She offered, kindly, to make it for us, in her preferred way. We accepted. We are not the same people we were before that holiday.

Every family meal abroad turns into a forty-five minute discussion about whether the local cuisine is suitable for my father, whose stomach has, since 1987, refused to accept anything more adventurous than a baked potato. We have toured Greece, Italy, and Spain, and my father has eaten, in each, a remarkably consistent menu of bread, plain pasta, and chips. He has, however, photographed every meal he refused to eat, for the album. The album is now twelve volumes long.

The family WhatsApp group has been arguing about the itinerary for our holiday for nine weeks.
