There are, as of this morning, three competing draft schedules, two breakaway sub-groups, and one open feud about whether we are going to the lake on Tuesday or Wednesday. Nobody has booked anything. The holiday is in five days. I have made my peace with the fact that we will, almost certainly, arrive somewhere and figure it out, in the way our family always does, with grim cheerfulness.

We agreed, before the holiday, that nobody would bring work emails on the trip. By dinner on the second night, my brother was on a call with a client in the garden, my sister was 'just checking one thing' on her laptop, and I had, in fact, written this very paragraph in the kitchen between cooking sausages. The agreement was, in retrospect, aspirational. We will sign it again next year. We will break it again next year. The cycle endures.

The forecast promised 'sunny intervals'. I have lived in this country long enough to know that 'sunny intervals' is a meteorologist's way of saying 'we genuinely have no idea, please pack everything'. I went out in a t-shirt. I came home in a t-shirt, a borrowed cardigan, a free umbrella from a charity shop, and a deep distrust of the institution of weather. The interval, when it arrived, lasted forty seconds and was witnessed by no one.

There is a particular weather presenter on the regional news who delivers a forecast of 'heavy rain and gusty winds' with the bright, beaming joy of a man announcing a lottery win. Every morning, hurricane-grade misery, delivered with a grin. I have come to depend on him. If he ever looked sad while saying 'mild and dry', I would assume the apocalypse had begun and start filling the bath with drinking water.

The app on my phone said there was an eighty percent chance of rain. I, a free-thinking adult, decided I was the twenty percent. I am writing this from a bus shelter, watching the rain come down with the conviction of someone settling an old grudge. The bus is nine minutes away. The bus shelter has three walls. The rain is arriving from the direction of the missing wall, personally, just for me.

The forecast described today as 'feels like four degrees'. I would like to know who is in charge of the 'feels like' temperature, because they have clearly never felt anything in their life. It does not feel like four degrees. It feels like a personal attack. It feels like the sky has read my diary. The actual temperature, apparently, is seven, which only makes the betrayal more elaborate.

We get one warm weekend a year in this country, and the entire population behaves as though the sun is a celebrity who has, against all odds, agreed to a brief public appearance. Every patch of grass becomes a festival. Men remove their shirts within the first eleven minutes, regardless of medical advice. Somebody buys a disposable barbecue and sets a bin on fire. It is glorious. It is chaos. By Monday it is raining again and we never speak of it.

The presenter pointed at a large swirling shape on the map and called it 'a band of unsettled weather'. I find the word 'unsettled' very generous. The weather was not unsettled. The weather had decided. The weather had made up its mind weeks ago and was now simply executing the plan. 'Unsettled' implies it could go either way. Nothing about three days of horizontal sleet suggests indecision.

There is a special category of British heatwave where the temperature reaches twenty-six degrees and the entire infrastructure of the nation immediately surrenders. The trains slow down out of respect. The roads, allegedly, melt. Newspapers run a photograph of a child eating an ice lolly with the headline 'PHEW!'. We are not built for warmth. We are a people optimised for drizzle, and any deviation is treated as a national emergency requiring a special broadcast.

I checked five different weather apps this morning, hoping to find one that agreed with my plans. One said sun. One said rain. One said 'partly cloudy'. One showed a small icon I have never seen before and could not identify, possibly a comet. The fifth simply showed a question mark, which I respected enormously, because at least it was being honest. I went out under the comet. The comet, as it turned out, was hail.

My grandmother does not trust the forecast and instead consults her left knee. The knee, she says, has a ninety percent accuracy rate, which is roughly forty points better than the national meteorological office. I used to laugh at this. Then last Tuesday her knee predicted a downpour while every screen in the house promised clear skies, and the heavens opened at precisely the hour she nominated. I now check the knee. The knee has a waiting list.

The forecaster ended the segment with 'and that's your weather, have a lovely day' immediately after describing forty-eight hours of unbroken thunderstorms. The cheerfulness was unshakeable. I do not know what training they receive, but they can deliver news of incoming meteorological doom with the warmth of a man handing you a birthday cake. I have started to find it sinister. Nobody should be that calm about that much sleet.

The hotel website described the room as having 'partial sea views'. The partial sea view, on arrival, turned out to be a sliver of grey water visible if you stood on the radiator, leaned out of the window at forty-five degrees, and looked left through a gap between a multi-storey car park and a building site. I stood on the radiator anyway. I saw the sea. I have, technically, no grounds for complaint, which is the most British outcome imaginable.

The hotel breakfast was advertised as a 'continental buffet'. I have now seen the continent in question, and it consists of three croissants under a heat lamp, a yoghurt that expired during a previous administration, and a coffee machine that produces a beige liquid the staff themselves refuse to make eye contact with. A man in a dressing gown took the last croissant ahead of me with the speed of an Olympic sprinter. I respected him. I also will never forgive him.

I booked a hotel based on a photograph of a sunlit room with a vast comfortable bed and a window full of mountains. The actual room had a bed the size of an ironing board, a window facing a brick wall four feet away, and a light fixture that flickered in a rhythm I am fairly sure was attempting to communicate something. I slept badly. I left a review saying 'cosy'. I am part of the problem.

The hotel room had a complicated panel of light switches by the door, none of them labelled. Over the course of one evening I turned on a light in the bathroom, a light I never located, a fan somewhere in the walls, and, on one memorable occasion, the television in the room next door. I gave up and lived by the glow of my phone for three nights, like a Victorian, but with worse posture and a charging cable.

I asked the receptionist if the hotel was quiet. She said, 'very quiet, sir,' with the warm confidence of a person who has never been lied to and never lied. The hotel was located, I discovered at 2 a.m., directly above a nightclub, beside a road frequented by emergency vehicles, and within earshot of what I can only assume was a competitive cockerel. I have written 'very quiet' on a sticky note. I keep it as a reminder that words mean nothing.

The hotel proudly advertised a 'fully equipped gym'. The fully equipped gym was a cupboard. Inside the cupboard was one exercise bike, manufactured during a decade I could not identify, missing a pedal, and facing a mirror positioned to ensure you watched yourself fail. There was also a single dumbbell, weight unknown, and a yoga mat that smelled of every previous guest's ambitions. I closed the cupboard. I went to the croissant table instead. The croissant table never lies about what it is.

My suitcase did not arrive at the airport. The airline assured me it would be 'delivered shortly'. The suitcase has now visited four countries I have never been to, and I have received tracking updates from it the way a parent receives postcards from a gap-year child. It was in Frankfurt. It was in a sorting facility. It was, briefly and inexplicably, in Casablanca. My suitcase is having a more eventful holiday than I am, and I packed all the good shorts.

The hotel pool was photographed, on the website, as a shimmering turquoise oasis lined with palm trees and serenity. The hotel pool, in reality, was a small rectangle of cold water located beside the car park, surrounded by white plastic chairs, and overlooked by every bedroom window in the building. Swimming in it felt less like a holiday and more like a public audition. I did one length. Everyone watched. I have retired from swimming.

I checked into the hotel at midnight after a delayed flight, exhausted, holding a single carrier bag. The receptionist, with great enthusiasm, embarked on a four-minute tour of the local area's attractions, the breakfast hours, the spa packages, and the history of the building, while I swayed gently in place like a man at sea. I retained none of it. I nodded forty times. I have, since, paid for a spa treatment I did not know I had booked.

The hotel offered a 'complimentary upgrade' which I accepted with delight. The upgrade was to a room on the ninth floor with a magnificent view, reached by a lift that was, the receptionist mentioned casually as I walked away, 'out of order until further notice'. I have carried my luggage up nine flights of stairs to enjoy a view I am now too tired to look at. I lay on the bed. I looked at the ceiling instead. The ceiling, in fairness, was also lovely.

I went to the garden centre to buy one bag of compost. I left three hours later having spent ninety pounds, owning a small olive tree, a wind chime, a ceramic frog of uncertain purpose, and a packet of seeds for a vegetable I have never eaten and cannot pronounce. The compost, the single item I went in for, I forgot entirely. I will have to go back. I am, I now understand, exactly the customer the garden centre was designed to capture.

The garden centre has a café, and the café is, somehow, always full of people in fleeces eating an enormous slice of cake at half past ten in the morning. I do not understand the economics of this. Nobody is buying plants. Everybody is having cake. I now believe the plants are merely a front, an elaborate decoy, and the true business of the garden centre is, and has always been, the sale of cake to people in fleeces.

I bought a plant labelled 'low maintenance, ideal for beginners'. The plant was dead within nine days. I returned to the garden centre, holding the brown remains aloft like evidence, and the assistant looked at it, looked at me, and said, very gently, 'what did you do to it?' I had watered it. That was, apparently, the crime. There is, it seems, a plant so low-maintenance that the act of caring for it constitutes abuse, and I had bought it.

There is a man who works at my local garden centre who knows the Latin name of every plant on the premises and will, if you make eye contact for longer than two seconds, tell you all of them. I asked him a simple question about a hanging basket. Forty minutes later I had learned about soil pH, the Victorian fern craze, and his views on slugs. I bought the basket purely to escape. I have not regretted it. The basket, and the friendship, are both thriving.

The garden centre sells gnomes. It sells a great number of gnomes, in a great number of poses, and I have never once seen a person buy a gnome, and yet the gnome stock never seems to diminish. I have begun to suspect the gnomes are not for sale at all. I think the gnomes are watching. I think the gnomes are the permanent staff, and the humans are seasonal. I bought a small one to be safe. He is in the car. He is facing forwards.

I asked the garden centre assistant whether a particular shrub would survive in my garden. She asked about my soil. I did not know. She asked about my light levels. I did not know. She asked which way my garden faced. I confidently said 'outwards'. She closed her eyes for a moment, the way professionals do, and then sold me a cactus, which she described as 'the only thing you cannot meaningfully harm'. I appreciated her honesty. The cactus and I are doing fine.

Every spring I visit the garden centre full of ambition. This year, I declare, will be the year of the vegetable patch. I buy the seeds, the trays, the little labels, the small fork. I arrange them lovingly in the shed. By August, I have produced two tomatoes and a courgette the size and density of a cricket ball. The courgette cost me, by my calculations, roughly fourteen pounds. I have eaten more expensive things, but never with such a sense of personal defeat.

The garden centre has a section called 'water features', and I made the mistake of walking through it. Now I want a small fountain. I do not need a small fountain. There is no logical argument for the fountain. But I have heard the gentle trickle, I have seen the stone heron, and a part of my brain that I cannot control has decided that my entire personality now depends on owning a fountain. My partner has been informed. My partner is concerned.

I overheard two people in the garden centre having a genuinely heated argument about whether a plant was an annual or a perennial. Voices were raised. A third person was drawn in. The staff watched from a distance, neither intervening nor surprised. I have never seen such passion in a retail environment. I left feeling that the world was, in its strange way, fine, if people could still feel that strongly about a flower's life expectancy on a Wednesday afternoon.

I went to buy bird seed and the garden centre had eleven different varieties, each promising to attract a specific and more impressive class of bird. I bought the most expensive one, the 'premium songbird blend', imagining a garden alive with goldfinches and warblers and gentle, tasteful birdsong. The blend has, so far, attracted forty pigeons and one extremely confident squirrel. The goldfinches, wherever they are, did not receive the memo. I have written to the manufacturer.

The wedding invitation said the dress code was 'smart casual', which is the most dangerous phrase in the English language. I arrived in chinos and a blazer, having agonised for an hour. Half the room was in three-piece suits. The other half was in jeans. The groom was in a kilt. Nobody was 'smart casual'. Smart casual does not exist. It is a trap laid by couples to watch their guests suffer, and I fell straight into it, holding a gift-wrapped toaster.

I was seated, at the wedding, at the table they politely call 'the singles table' and everyone else calls 'the table of people the couple could not figure out where else to put'. I was placed between a man who only spoke about his allotment and a woman who was, it emerged over the soup, the groom's former driving instructor. We had nothing in common. By the dessert, however, we were a tight unit, bonded by exclusion, and we are now, somehow, going on a group holiday.

The best man's speech began with the words 'I'll keep this brief' and continued, against all known laws of time, for twenty-six minutes. He told a story about a stag do that I am fairly sure was a criminal confession. He referenced four in-jokes that nobody in the room understood, including, judging by his face, the groom. He cried twice. We clapped, eventually, out of relief rather than appreciation, and the relief was genuine and deep.

There is a moment at every wedding reception, roughly forty minutes into the dancing, when a particular song comes on and every person over the age of fifty-five rushes the dance floor with a speed and conviction they have not shown all evening. The young people retreat to the edges, holding drinks, suddenly shy. The older generation owns the floor. They know the moves. They have known them for decades. We are merely guests at their event now.

I was asked to do a reading at a friend's wedding. I practised for two weeks. I knew the poem by heart. I stood up, walked to the front, looked out at one hundred and forty expectant faces, and my voice came out as the high, uncertain whisper of a frightened child. I read the entire poem to the second row of chairs. The couple said it was lovely. They are kind people. They are also, I suspect, lying, and I have decided to let them.

The wedding had a photo booth, which is a small fabric box designed to extract the dignity of every guest in a strictly time-limited fashion. By the end of the night, the photo album contained one hundred images of grown adults wearing oversized novelty sunglasses and feather boas, pulling faces, holding cardboard signs that said things like 'Team Bride'. We are, all of us, professionals. We have mortgages. The photo booth does not care, and frankly neither did we, by then.

At the wedding buffet, there was a queue, and within that queue there was a man who took an architecturally improbable amount of food onto one plate. It was a feat of structural engineering. Cocktail sausages balanced on coleslaw, supported by a foundation of quiche, the whole thing reaching towards the chandeliers. We all watched. We all judged. We were all, deep down, taking notes for our own return trip.

The couple had a 'wishing well' instead of a gift list, which is a wedding's polite way of asking for cash. I put an envelope into a small decorative barrel. The decorative barrel was already heaving with envelopes. I thought about the bride and groom, later that night, sitting on their hotel bed, opening forty envelopes, counting the contents like a pair of small, well-dressed bank tellers. It is the least romantic possible end to a romantic day, and I find it strangely wonderful.

I caught the bouquet at a wedding entirely by accident. I was not trying. I was, in fact, attempting to move out of the way of the bouquet, and it landed in my hands through no fault of my own. The room cheered. My partner of eleven years, standing beside me, raised an eyebrow that contained an entire conversation. We have not discussed it. The bouquet is, currently, in a vase on the windowsill, watching us, waiting.

The wedding ceremony was outdoors, in a field, in June, which the couple described in the invitation as 'romantic' and which the weather described as 'an opportunity'. It rained from a clear sky out of pure spite. One hundred guests sat on hay bales under a borrowed assortment of umbrellas, watching the couple exchange vows while a marquee, somewhere behind us, made the sound of a ship in distress. It was, everyone agreed afterwards, the best wedding they had ever attended.

I ordered a 'medium' jumper. The medium jumper arrived and would comfortably fit a confident toddler. I checked the size chart. The size chart insisted I had ordered correctly. I am now in a silent dispute with a brand's idea of the human body, and I have lost. The jumper has been re-gifted to my nephew, who is delighted, and who is, I should mention, six years old. The brand has emailed me to ask how I would rate my experience.

I added one essential item to my online basket. Then the website, in its quiet wisdom, showed me 'customers also bought', and I, a weak and easily led creature, agreed with every single one of those customers. Three hours later my basket contained a fondue set, a book about Antarctic exploration, a novelty doorstop, and a lamp shaped like a cactus. The original essential item had, somewhere in the journey, been removed. I have ordered everything except the thing I needed.

The product had four thousand reviews and a near-perfect rating, so I bought it with confidence. It arrived broken. I went back to read the reviews more carefully and discovered that the four thousand glowing reviews were all for a completely different product, a garden hose, somehow attached to the listing for an electric kettle. The kettle itself had one review. The review said, simply, 'do not'. I had not scrolled far enough. I never scroll far enough.

I left one pair of shoes in an online basket and closed the tab. I have since been pursued across the entire internet by those shoes. They appear beside news articles. They appear inside videos. They appeared, last night, in an advert during a programme about medieval cathedrals, which felt like a stretch even for them. The shoes will not let me go. I am beginning to think the only way to be free of the shoes is to buy the shoes, which is, of course, exactly the plan.

The delivery window was 'between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.', which is not a window. A window is a small, defined opening. That is an entire waking day. I waited in. I did not shower, in case the doorbell rang. I did not start anything that could not be abandoned in eleven seconds. At 7:52 p.m., having achieved nothing all day, I received a notification that the parcel had been 'left in a safe place'. The safe place was the recycling bin. The bin was collected the next morning.

I bought a desk online described as 'easy to assemble' and shown in a photograph being built, effortlessly, by a smiling woman holding a single small tool. The box that arrived contained two hundred and fourteen components, a wordless instruction manual that appeared to have been translated by a fax machine, and a tiny metal key for a process that is never explained. The smiling woman, wherever she is, lied to me, and I think about her often.

I have a relationship with a delivery driver I have never met. He knows my house. He knows the gate sticks. He knows to leave parcels behind the green bin, not the black one, a distinction I communicated through a series of increasingly elaborate notes taped to the door. We have never spoken. We have never seen each other. He is, by volume of trust placed in him, one of the most significant people in my life, and his name, according to the app, is Dave.

I ordered a single phone charger and it arrived in a cardboard box large enough to relocate a family of badgers. The charger, a small object weighing approximately nothing, sat alone in the centre of this vast space, cushioned by an extravagant amount of paper, like a tiny king in an enormous throne room. I felt the universe was trying to tell me something about scale, and proportion, and the modern world, but mostly I felt I now had a very large empty box and no clear plan.

The website assured me the item was 'almost gone' with 'only 2 left in stock', a small red message designed to make my heart race. So I bought it, urgently, before the alleged scarcity could claim it. I returned to the website a week later. There were still 'only 2 left in stock'. There have always been 'only 2 left in stock'. There will always be 'only 2 left in stock'. The number 2, on this website, is not a quantity. It is a personality.

I tried to return an item, and the returns process required me to print a label. I do not own a printer. Nobody under the age of fifty owns a printer. I went to a friend's house to use her printer, which was out of ink, then to a library, which had a printer but a queue, then to a shop that charged me more to print the label than the item itself had cost. The jumper, which did not fit, is now mine forever. We have made peace.

I bought a houseplant to bring life and calm into my flat. The houseplant has, instead, become a source of constant low-grade anxiety. I check it the way other people check the stock market. Is that leaf yellowing? Is it drooping or merely resting? Does it want more light, less light, or simply to be left alone, like the rest of us? I have a degree. I have a job. I am being emotionally managed by a fern.

My monstera has produced a new leaf, and I have told seven people about it. I sent photographs. I described the process of the leaf unfurling as though narrating a moon landing. Two of those people do not own plants. One of them, I now realise, does not even like me very much. But the leaf is magnificent, and I have decided that anyone unwilling to celebrate a leaf with me is not, fundamentally, my kind of person.

I own a plant that the shop described as 'unkillable'. I have killed it. Twice. I have bought the same unkillable plant on two separate occasions and reduced each one, through no intentional effort, to a small brown reminder of my own limitations. The shop assistant, on my third visit, did not say anything. He simply handed me a plastic plant, gently, with the look of a man releasing a bird that cannot fly. The plastic plant is thriving. I water it anyway.

I have given all of my houseplants names, and I am not going to apologise for it. There is Susan, who is dramatic and droops at the slightest provocation. There is Gerald, who is steady, reliable, and asks for nothing. There is a small succulent called The Intern, who I am not sure has a future here. I talk to them. They do not talk back, which is, frankly, one of the main reasons I prefer them to most of my colleagues.

My flat now contains forty-one houseplants. I did not plan this. It happened the way debt happens, slowly, then all at once. I cannot walk through the living room without performing a small careful dance. Guests comment on it. Some of them say 'jungle' warmly, and some say 'jungle' with a flicker of concern. I have run out of windowsills. I have started, and I want to be honest about this, eyeing the windowsills of other people.

I went away for a long weekend and arranged an elaborate watering system for my plants involving string, two upturned bottles, and a level of confidence not supported by any prior experience. I returned to find one plant flooded, one bone dry, and a third somehow knocked clean off the shelf and lying on the carpet like a fallen soldier. The system had not worked. The string had achieved nothing. The plants and I no longer trust each other, and the trip was not even that good.

I followed a houseplant influencer online and now I feel, daily, that my plants are underachieving. Her monstera is the size of a small car. Her windowsills overflow with abundance. Her flat looks like a botanical garden that has won an award. My plants, by comparison, look tired, like commuters. I do not know what she does. I suspect lighting, both literal and photographic. I have unfollowed her. My plants and I are recovering our self-esteem together, quietly.

Someone gave me a cutting from their plant, and I now feel responsible for it in a way that keeps me up at night. It is not just a plant. It is a piece of a friendship, in water, on my kitchen counter, and if it dies it will be a metaphor, and the friend will know, and there will be a small unspoken sadness between us forever. The cutting has grown one tiny root. I have wept with relief. This is not, I am aware, a normal way to live.

My cat regards every new houseplant I bring home as a personal challenge and a salad. I have placed plants on high shelves, behind barriers, in rooms with closed doors. The cat finds them. The cat always finds them. I have, at this point, simply accepted that I am running a small, doomed botanical garden and the cat is its only critic, its primary threat, and the closest thing it has to a head of security, all at once.

I repotted a plant for the first time, having watched a calming video in which a person did it gracefully on a clean wooden table. My version involved soil on the floor, soil on the sofa, soil somehow on the ceiling, a plant looking deeply betrayed, and me, on my knees, apologising aloud to a root system. The video did not prepare me for the emotional labour. The plant survived. We do not discuss the incident.

My fitness tracker congratulated me, with a small celebratory buzz, for completing ten thousand steps. I had not been exercising. I had been pacing the kitchen for forty minutes, on the phone, arguing with an energy company. The tracker does not know the difference between achievement and despair. It thinks I had a wonderful, active day. In a sense, the tracker is the only one of us still feeling positive about it, and I have not had the heart to correct it.

My watch buzzed and said, 'Time to stand!' in a cheerful tone. I was at a funeral. I have never wanted to throw a small electronic device into a hedge with such intensity. The watch does not understand context. The watch believes that all sitting is laziness and all standing is virtue. The watch has never been to a funeral. The watch knows nothing of grief, or of dignity, or of the inappropriate timing of its own optimism.

I went for a brisk twenty-minute walk and forgot to wear my fitness tracker. As far as my watch is concerned, that walk did not happen. It was not logged. It does not count. I genuinely considered walking the route again, wearing the watch this time, simply so the effort would be recorded somewhere. I have become a man who exercises not for his body, but for the approval of a small piece of plastic on his wrist. I am not proud. But I did do the second walk.

My fitness tracker has informed me that my sleep last night was 'poor'. I am aware. I was there. I lived through the entire poor sleep in real time, minute by minute, watching the ceiling. I did not require a device to wake me up and tell me, first thing in the morning, that I had slept badly. The tracker reports my failures back to me as news. I have started, quietly, to resent the tracker. It rates my rest. It judges my night. It is, frankly, getting above itself.

My fitness tracker detected my heart rate spiking and asked, with concern, if I was doing a workout. I was not doing a workout. I was reading an email from my manager. The tracker, helpfully, offered to start logging the activity. I declined. I do not want a permanent record of how my body responds to the phrase 'quick chat?'. Some metrics are better left uncollected. Some data, once gathered, can never be unknown.

I am in a step competition with my brother, mediated entirely by our fitness trackers, and it has destroyed my relationship with the outdoors. I no longer go for walks. I go on missions. I pace the platform at the train station. I take the long way to the bin. Last Sunday I walked in circles around my own kitchen island for half an hour while a documentary played, purely to overtake him before midnight. He won anyway. He has a dog.

My watch awarded me a small digital trophy for 'most active month'. I held the watch up to the light. I examined the trophy. It was a tiny golden image of a flame, and it represented nothing, and it could not be sold, displayed, or eaten. And yet I felt a flicker of genuine pride. A corporation has discovered that I will, apparently, jog up a hill in the rain for a cartoon of a flame. The corporation knows me better than my own parents do.

The tracker buzzed to tell me I had been 'inactive for too long' while I was, in fact, in the middle of a long-haul flight, strapped into a seat, somewhere over Greenland. There was nowhere to go. There was nothing to be done. The tracker, undeterred, suggested a brisk walk. I looked out of the window at a vast and empty ice sheet, thirty-eight thousand feet below, and concluded that my watch and I have very different understandings of what is possible.

I waved my arm enthusiastically while telling a story at dinner, and my fitness tracker logged it as 'elliptical training'. According to my watch, I burned a hundred and twelve calories describing a problem I had at the bank. I am not going to correct the data. I have decided to lean into it. From now on, all of my exercise will be storytelling, and I will become extremely fit purely through the medium of strong opinions and large gestures.

The fitness tracker has a feature where it shows you, on a little graph, how you compare to 'people like you'. People like me, apparently, are doing extremely well. People like me are running marathons and climbing things. I do not feel like people like me. I feel like a person who has been mistakenly grouped with the wrong people, and I would like the graph to find me a new, slower, more honest peer group, possibly one that also enjoys sitting down.

Somebody at the office has, for the third time this week, left a single plate in the communal sink. Not washed. Not in the dishwasher. Just placed there, gently, as an offering. A passive-aggressive note has appeared above the sink. A counter-note has appeared below it. We are now, as a department, conducting an entire silent war through laminated paper, and the plate, the original plate, the cause of it all, remains exactly where it was, watching its empire grow.

There is a yoghurt in the office fridge with a name written on it in large, defensive capital letters. The name has been underlined. Twice. The yoghurt has been in there for what I estimate to be eleven days. Nobody will touch it, because it is named, and to take a named yoghurt is to commit the gravest crime in office society. The yoghurt has, through sheer force of labelling, achieved a kind of immortality. It will outlast us all.

The office microwave is the site of our greatest cultural disagreement. There are those who believe in standing patiently and watching their food rotate. There are those who walk away and return precisely on time, like clockwork. And there is one man, a man I will not name, who reheats fish in it at 12:30 every single day, knowing exactly what he is doing, knowing the consequences, and choosing, with full awareness, to do it anyway. He is the office's only true anarchist.

Someone in the office finishes the milk and returns the empty carton to the fridge. They do this every time. They are among us. They walk past us in the corridor, they attend the same meetings, they say good morning, and then, when no one is watching, they place an empty milk carton back on the shelf as if it still has purpose. I have made coffee with no milk so many times that I have, frankly, started to acquire a taste for despair.

The office has a single good mug. It is the right size, the right weight, the handle sits perfectly. There are forty staff and one good mug, and the entire social hierarchy of the company is, secretly, organised around who gets to use it. I have it now. I am drinking from it. I am writing this from a meeting, holding the good mug, and the man across the table keeps glancing at it. He knows. He wants it. He cannot have it. Not today.

It was someone's birthday and a cake appeared in the office kitchen with a small handwritten sign reading 'help yourself'. By the time I arrived, at 2 p.m., the cake had been reduced to a thin smear of icing and a few crumbs of dignity. The knife was still there, standing upright in the wreckage, like a flag planted by the last person to give up. I had a crumb. I told the birthday colleague it was delicious. We both knew I was being kind.

There is a drawer in the office kitchen that contains forty-five identical teaspoons and not one single fork. There has never been a fork. Forks arrive, are used once, and vanish into a dimension that only forks can access. People bring forks from home and those forks, too, are claimed. I have stopped fighting it. I now eat my lunchtime salad with a teaspoon, slowly, with the patient resignation of a man who has accepted the rules of a universe he did not design.

Management installed a fancy coffee machine in the office kitchen, a gleaming chrome device with eleven buttons and no instructions. Nobody knows how to use it correctly. We have all developed our own private rituals, our own button sequences, passed down quietly from senior staff to new hires like sacred knowledge. The machine produces, regardless of which buttons are pressed, the same brown liquid. We thank it anyway. We are grateful. We have been broken.

Somebody has put a sign on the office fridge that says 'CLEAR OUT YOUR ITEMS BY FRIDAY OR THEY WILL BE BINNED'. It is a threat. It is a deadline. And every single person in this office, all forty of us, has read that sign, felt a flicker of anxiety, and done absolutely nothing. On Monday the fridge will be untouched, the sign will still be there, and a new, angrier sign will appear beneath it. This is how civilisations end.

The office kettle takes four minutes to boil and during those four minutes you are trapped in the kitchen with whoever else is waiting, forced into conversation. I have learned more about my colleague Brian's caravan, his back, and his ongoing dispute with a neighbour over a hedge, in four-minute increments, than I know about my own family. The kettle is, in a sense, the heart of the office. It is also, undeniably, far too slow, and Brian is far too keen.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I have been learning French for eight months using an app, and I am now extremely confident in exactly four areas: I can tell you that the cat is on the table, I can express that I would like a coffee, I can announce that it is raining, and I can declare, with great fluency, that the boy is sad. Whether I will ever stand in a Parisian café and need all four of these facts to be simultaneously true, I do not know. I am prepared, regardless.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: The language app sends me a notification every evening that begins encouraging and grows, over a missed week, genuinely menacing. It started with 'time for your lesson!'. Then 'don't break your streak!'. Then a small cartoon owl looking, frankly, disappointed in me. Last night the notification simply said 'these reminders don't seem to be working' in a tone of quiet defeat, and I have never felt so seen, or so judged, by a piece of software.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I went to Italy, ready to deploy six months of evening Italian classes. I walked confidently into a bakery, prepared a sentence in my head, delivered it flawlessly, and the baker responded with a torrent of actual, real, fast Italian, spoken by a real Italian person, and I understood not one single word of it. I had practised speaking. I had not practised the terrifying part where they speak back. I bought, by pointing, a loaf I did not want.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: My Spanish textbook is teaching me phrases for situations I do not anticipate encountering. So far I can describe a bullfight, complain about a hotel room's air conditioning, and discuss, at length, my fictional uncle's career as an architect. I cannot, however, ask where the toilet is, which feels like an oversight of staggering proportions. The textbook has its priorities. They are not my priorities. My uncle is not even real.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I told my German tutor I wanted to sound more natural. She said the first step was to learn the word for 'um'. Apparently every language has its own specific filler noise, its own particular sound of a person thinking, and using the wrong one marks you instantly as a foreigner. I have now spent two weeks practising the German 'um'. I can do the 'um' perfectly. I cannot do any of the actual sentences, but I can hesitate like a true Berliner.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I have been learning Japanese, and the writing system has three separate alphabets, one of which exists, as far as I can tell, purely to humble me. Every time I feel I am making progress, I encounter a new character that looks like a small, complicated house and means something like 'the feeling of mild regret on a Tuesday'. I am not progressing through the language. I am being slowly, gently introduced to the full scale of my own ignorance.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: My language app celebrated my 'one hundred day streak' with great fanfare, a shower of digital confetti, and a small trophy. In those hundred days I have done, on average, one minute of study per day, usually in bed, half asleep, tapping the easiest possible answers. I have a hundred-day streak and I cannot hold a conversation. The streak is not a measure of learning. The streak is a measure of my fear of disappointing an owl.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I joined a conversation group to practise my French, and discovered that everyone else in the group was significantly better than me, including, somehow, a man who had only started two weeks earlier. I spent the first session nodding, smiling, and saying 'oui, oui, c'est ça' to statements I had not understood, which is, I am told, also how I get through most meetings in English. At least the skill transfers.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: I tried to learn a language by changing my phone to that language, a tip I read online from a confident stranger. I now cannot operate my phone. I do not know what any of the buttons do. I have accidentally enabled three settings I cannot find again to disable. I have, in a sense, learned a great deal, mostly about panic, and about how much of my life is held together by recognising the shapes of words rather than reading them. The phone is in Portuguese. I am not.

subtopic: learning a language as an adult
sentence: My Italian teacher asked me to introduce myself to the class. I had prepared. I stood, I said my name, my age, my profession, and then, reaching the end of my prepared material with thirty seconds of attention still trained on me, I panicked and announced, in confident Italian, that I had four sisters. I do not have four sisters. I have no sisters. I now have a relationship with this class built entirely on a foundation of imaginary siblings I will have to maintain for a year.

Every supermarket trolley has, somewhere in its history, sustained a wheel injury, and the supermarket distributes these wounded trolleys to customers using a system based, I am convinced, on cruelty. My trolley today wished to go only left. We travelled the entire shop at a forty-five degree angle, me wrestling it like a man steering a small distressed boat, while it tried, persistently, lovingly, to reunite me with the freezer aisle I had already visited.

I put a pound coin in the trolley to release it from its long chain of identical brothers. At that moment I was bound to the trolley by an economic contract. That trolley was mine. I was responsible for it. The relief, at the end of the shop, of slotting it back and reclaiming my pound, is one of the purest emotions available to a modern adult, and I am not ashamed to say I look forward to it more than I look forward to most of the shopping itself.

There is a particular trolley abandoned in the middle of the car park, far from any car, far from the trolley bay, sitting alone in a parking space like a small metal monument to human laziness. It has been there for three days. We all see it. We all swerve around it. Nobody returns it. It is becoming, slowly, a landmark. I gave a delivery driver directions yesterday using the trolley as a reference point. It has earned its place.

I selected a trolley, tested it for wheel integrity by pushing it back and forth twice in the entrance, declared it sound, and set off. Within eleven seconds, the moment it bore the weight of actual groceries, it revealed its true character: a deafening rattle, a persistent leftward drift, and a single wheel that no longer rotated but merely scraped. The test had been a lie. The trolley had performed wellness. The trolley had deceived me, and I respect its patience.

There is an unspoken supermarket law that two people who know each other will, inevitably, leave their trolleys parked end to end across the entire width of an aisle while they catch up. They will discuss a christening. They will discuss a hip operation. And behind them, a quiet queue of polite people forms, nobody willing to say anything, all of us silently aging, waiting for the conversation about the hip to reach its natural conclusion so we can reach the pasta.

I went to the supermarket for three items and took a trolley anyway, telling myself I would only use a small corner of it. I now own forty items. The trolley is full. The trolley was not a container, it turns out. The trolley was an invitation, a vast steel suggestion, a question the supermarket asks you, which is, 'what if you bought all of this?', and to which I, weak and suggestible, answered 'yes, alright then'.

A small child has been placed in the trolley seat by a parent ahead of me, and that child has spent the entire shop facing backwards, making direct, unbroken eye contact with me. We have been together for twenty minutes. I have followed this family through four aisles purely by coincidence and now we are bonded. The child has not blinked. The child knows something. I have started to find the dairy section emotionally intense.

It was windy in the car park, and I watched a runaway trolley achieve a genuine turn of speed, gliding majestically and entirely unmanned across three parking bays toward a parked car. A man dropped his bags and sprinted to intercept it, diving, catching it inches from the bumper, a true hero. Nobody applauded. I wanted to applaud. The British capacity for not acknowledging quiet heroism is, itself, a kind of heroism.

The mini supermarket near my flat only has baskets, no trolleys, and so I am regularly forced to do a full week's shop carrying a basket that grows, with each item, into an instrument of torture. By the till, the basket weighs the same as a small dog, the handle has carved a line into my palm, and my arm has stretched, I am fairly sure, by several centimetres. I refuse, on principle, to make two trips. The principle is winning. My arm is not.

I returned my trolley to the trolley bay and discovered that the act of slotting it neatly into the line, nesting it perfectly with its fellows, gave me a small and disproportionate sense of accomplishment. In a day otherwise devoid of clear wins, the trolley had clicked into place, the chain had connected, and I had, briefly, completed something. I stood there a moment too long. A man waiting behind me cleared his throat. I had been savouring the trolley. I left.

I attempted a layer cake for my mother's birthday. The internet showed a photograph of three perfectly level sponges stacked with mathematical precision. My three sponges came out of the oven shaped, respectively, like a hill, a valley, and a confused geological event. The finished cake leans. It leans in a way that suggests intent. My mother said it had 'character'. I have decided that 'character', from a mother, about a cake, is the gentlest possible word for 'tragedy'.

The recipe said to 'fold in' the flour. I do not know what folding is. I have watched videos. I have read descriptions. I have made a motion with a spatula that I believed, with great hope, to be folding. The cake came out dense enough to be used as a doorstop, or possibly a defensive weapon. Somewhere there is a person who knows how to fold flour, and that person is not me, and the gap between us is, I now understand, unbridgeable.

I baked bread. The internet promised a golden, crusty loaf with an open, airy crumb. What emerged from my oven was a small, dense, beige sphere with the structural properties of a cricket ball and the weight of a planet. I knocked on the bottom of it, as instructed, to check if it was done. It made the sound of a door. I have, in a sense, baked a small piece of furniture, and I am going to eat it, because I am not made of money.

I have learned, the hard way, that 'a pinch of salt' and 'a cup of salt' produce dramatically different biscuits. I misread a recipe in a moment of distraction. The biscuits were, technically, edible, in the sense that a person could put one in their mouth. My family each took a small bite, in unison, and then a strange silence fell over the kitchen, a silence I will remember for the rest of my life. We do not, in this house, discuss the salt biscuits.

I tried to make macarons because a television programme made it look like a charming afternoon activity. Macarons, I have since discovered, are not a charming afternoon activity. Macarons are a test of the human spirit. My first batch cracked. My second batch was hollow. My third batch fused into a single continental macaron the size of a dinner plate. I have decided that macarons are not food. Macarons are a hazing ritual, and I have failed to be hazed.

The recipe said to bake the cake until a skewer 'comes out clean'. I inserted a skewer. It came out clean. I removed the cake, confident, triumphant. The cake was raw in the centre. The skewer had lied. The skewer and the recipe had conspired against me. I now bake everything for an additional, defensive twenty minutes regardless of instructions, and my cakes are dry, and my trust in cutlery is, I think, permanently broken.

I decided to make a birthday cake from scratch rather than buy one, in a moment of misplaced confidence and economy. By the time I had purchased the specialist tin, the piping bag, the food colouring, the nozzle set, and replaced the smoke alarm battery that I had removed in a panic, the homemade cake had cost roughly four times the price of a shop cake, and looked, in a generous light, like something a shop would have rejected.

I attempted to ice a cake smoothly. I had a small flat tool, and I had watched a calm professional glide it around a cake until the surface gleamed. My attempt produced a cake that looked as though the icing had been applied during an earthquake, by a stranger, in the dark. There are peaks. There are valleys. There is one area I have simply covered with a strategically placed strawberry. The strawberry is not decoration. The strawberry is hiding something.

I made a trifle. Trifle, I had assumed, was forgiving, being essentially a controlled collapse of several puddings into one bowl. I was wrong. My layers migrated. The custard breached the sponge. The jelly never set and instead became a sort of sweet weather system within the dish. By the time I served it, the trifle had homogenised into a single beige experience. My guests ate it with spoons and brave faces, and one of them called it 'rustic', which I have decided to treasure.

I forgot to put sugar in the cake. I followed every other step with great care. I greased the tin, I preheated the oven, I folded, I leveled. And then I served, to four guests, a beautiful, golden, perfectly risen cake that tasted, against all expectation, of nothing whatsoever. It was the saddest cake ever made. It looked like joy and tasted like a damp Tuesday. We ate it all. Nobody mentioned the sugar. They are good people.

The self-checkout machine has, once again, accused me of placing an 'unexpected item in the bagging area'. The unexpected item is my own shopping bag. The machine knew I would bring a bag. The machine asked me, moments ago, if I had a bag. And yet the presence of the bag has shocked it to its core. I now stand with my arms raised slightly, away from all surfaces, like a man being searched, waiting for an attendant to come and forgive me for the crime of grocery shopping.

I bought a single bottle of wine at the self-checkout and the machine, with no warning, locked itself, flashed a red light, and announced loudly to the entire shop that it required 'approval'. I stood there, a grown adult, publicly suspected, while a sixteen-year-old attendant strolled over at the pace of someone who has all the power and knows it, glanced at me, pressed a button, and walked away without a word. I have never felt younger, or guiltier, in my life.

The self-checkout machine speaks to me in a relentlessly cheerful voice that does not match the situation we are in together. 'Please wait for assistance!' it chirps, while I am trapped, mid-transaction, with a queue forming and a frozen pizza slowly thawing in my hand. The voice does not care. The voice was recorded years ago, by a calm person, in a quiet room, who could not have imagined the chaos their pleasant tone would one day narrate.

I tried to weigh some loose mushrooms at the self-checkout, and the machine demanded I select the type of mushroom from a list of forty-three mushroom-related options. I did not know what kind of mushroom I had bought. I had simply chosen 'the brown ones'. I scrolled. I panicked. I selected, eventually, something at random, and I am now fairly sure I have been charged the price of a rare and ceremonial fungus. I did not go back. I could not face the list again.

There is one attendant supervising eight self-checkout machines, and that attendant is the busiest, most powerful, and most weary person in the entire building. They move between the machines in a constant loop, approving wine, calming error messages, untangling crises, summoned by a relentless chorus of flashing lights. They never rest. They are the lone shepherd of a flock of malfunctioning robots, and they earn, I would guess, a wage that does not begin to reflect the spiritual cost.

I scanned an item and the machine could not find the price. It froze. It thought. It displayed a small spinning circle of contemplation. And then, having found nothing, it simply asked me, the customer, with what felt like genuine hope, 'how much was this?'. I do not work here. I do not know the price. We stood there, the machine and I, two confused entities, each waiting for the other to take responsibility, and I felt, for a moment, real sympathy for it.

I have developed, over years of practice, an elaborate technique for using the self-checkout: I bag slowly, I place each item with deliberate gentleness, I avoid sudden movements, I do not breathe near the scale. It is less like shopping and more like defusing a bomb. And still, despite all my care, all my reverence, the machine will, at some random moment, decide that I have done something terrible, and the red light will summon the shepherd, and I will once again be a suspect.

The machine asked, 'Do you have a loyalty card?'. I did not. It asked, 'Would you like to sign up for a loyalty card?'. I did not. It then displayed a screen extolling the benefits of the loyalty card, with photographs of happy people, clearly loyal, holding their cards aloft. I declined again. The machine paused, and in that pause I felt judged, as though I had let down not just the machine but an entire community of cardholders who had welcomed me, and whom I had spurned.

At the end of the transaction, the machine asked me to rate my self-checkout experience by pressing one of four faces, ranging from a beaming smile to a face of profound sorrow. I had just spent six minutes being accused of theft by a robot. I pressed the sad face firmly. The machine thanked me, brightly, for my feedback, and I understood, in that moment, that the feedback goes nowhere, helps no one, and exists purely so the machine can feel it has listened.

I watched a man, two machines over, lose an argument with a self-checkout so completely that he simply stopped, set down his basket, raised both hands in the universal gesture of surrender, and walked out of the shop, leaving his half-scanned groceries behind. He did not look back. He did not collect his bag. The machine, still cheerful, still hopeful, continued to ask the empty air whether it had brought its own bag. The man, I think, made the right choice.

The instruction booklet for the bookcase contained no words at all, only diagrams of a small, faceless cartoon person assembling the bookcase with serene ease. The cartoon person never struggles. The cartoon person never has a screw left over. The cartoon person has, in panel six, a fully built bookcase and, I assume, a deep inner peace. I hate the cartoon person. I am, three hours in, surrounded by panels two through five, and the cartoon person is mocking me from the future.

I laid out all the furniture pieces on the living room floor in neat, organised rows, the way a confident person would, the way a person in control would. I counted the screws. I identified the panels. And then I began, and within twenty minutes the neat rows were gone, the floor was chaos, and I was holding a wooden dowel and a hex key and a piece labelled 'F', and I could not, for the life of me, locate piece 'A', the foundation, the beginning of everything.

I finished assembling the chest of drawers, stood back, wiped my brow, and felt the deep satisfaction of a job completed. Then I noticed, on the carpet, a single screw. One screw. Unaccounted for. The chest of drawers appeared, by every visible measure, to be finished and stable. But that screw belonged somewhere. That screw had a purpose. And now I must live, every day, with a chest of drawers that contains a mystery, a hidden weakness, a screw-shaped question I will never answer.

I built the entire wardrobe with great care, attaching every panel, tightening every bolt, and only at the very end, stepping back to admire it, did I see that the large decorative front panel, the one that faces the room, was on backwards. The plain side faced out. The good side faced the wall. To fix it would mean dismantling everything. I have decided, instead, that this wardrobe is minimalist, that it is a statement, and that I meant to do this.

The furniture instructions clearly stated 'two people recommended'. I am one person. I am a confident, capable person, and I decided that 'recommended' was merely a suggestion, a polite formality. I was wrong. I have now spent forty minutes pinned beneath a partially assembled bed frame, holding two panels together with my feet while reaching for a screwdriver with my teeth. 'Recommended', I now understand, was a warning, dressed up in gentle language, and I did not listen.

The little tool that comes in the box, the small flat metal key shaped like a stickman, is the only tool that will fit the bolts, and it is designed, I am certain, to inflict the maximum possible damage on the human hand. By bolt number nine, my palm bore a perfect red impression of the tool, a small medal of suffering. There are forty bolts. I have considered buying a proper screwdriver. But the proper screwdriver does not fit. Nothing fits but the stickman. We suffer together.

I have reached step fourteen of the assembly instructions and discovered that step fourteen requires a part I attached, irreversibly, during step six. To proceed, I must go back. To go back, I must undo six panels, four dowels, and my own sense of progress. I sat on the floor for a while, among the wooden pieces, and considered my life. Then I undid step six. The cartoon person in the diagram does not have to deal with this. The cartoon person never goes back.

I confidently told my partner that I did not need the instructions, that the desk was 'intuitive', that I would simply assemble it through reason and common sense. The desk is now a structure that defies the known principles of furniture. It has an asymmetry that cannot be explained. One drawer opens into another drawer. My partner has not said anything. My partner has simply placed the discarded instruction booklet, smoothed flat, on the floor beside me, and left the room.

The flat-pack box weighed slightly more than I do and was labelled, by a comedian at the warehouse, 'easy lift'. I dragged it from the front door to the living room across forty minutes and one pulled muscle. I have not yet opened the box. The box is in the middle of the room. I am sitting on the box, recovering, and the box has become, for now, the most substantial piece of furniture I own. I may simply keep the box. The box, at least, is finished.

I assembled a small side table and it stands, and it holds objects, and by every functional definition it is a side table. But it wobbles. There is a wobble. I have tightened every bolt twice. I have placed a folded piece of card under one leg. The wobble persists, faint but eternal, and now every time I put a cup of tea on the table I perform a small ritual of placing it gently, gently, in the centre, as if the table and I have agreed to never speak of its flaw.

The neighbourhood group chat began, three years ago, as a sensible forum for reporting suspicious activity and lost cats. It is now, primarily, a stage for one man, Derek, who posts daily updates on the activity of a fox. The fox has crossed the road. The fox has been near the bins. The fox, this morning, 'gave Derek a look'. Forty-seven adults receive these notifications. Nobody asked for them. Nobody can leave. We are all hostages of Derek and the fox.

Someone posted in the neighbourhood group chat asking if anyone else had heard a strange noise last night. Within forty minutes there were ninety-one replies. The noise had been variously identified as a fox, an owl, a boiler, a burglar, fireworks, a car, the wind, and, by one resident with great confidence, 'a portent'. Nobody knows what the noise was. Nobody ever will. But the community has never felt closer, united by a sound none of us can describe.

A woman posted a photograph of a parked car in the neighbourhood group chat with the caption 'does anyone know whose car this is????'. The car was parked legally, on a public road, doing nothing. But the four question marks carried a menace, an accusation, and within an hour the chat had spiralled into a debate about parking, entitlement, and the moral decline of the street. The car, throughout, simply sat there, parked, innocent, the unwitting villain of our evening.

Every December, the neighbourhood group chat erupts into a passionate, sprawling argument about whose Christmas lights are 'too much'. There are traditionalists. There are maximalists. There is one house with an inflatable snowman the size of a small building, and that snowman has been, for two weeks, the single most divisive figure in local politics. Marriages are quieter than this chat. Nobody discusses anything else. The snowman, gently glowing, does not know the chaos it has caused.

Someone new joined the neighbourhood group chat and made the mistake of introducing themselves cheerfully and asking for restaurant recommendations. This was treated as an act of profound naivety. The chat is not for that. The chat is for bins, suspicious vans, and the fox. The newcomer received one reply, from Derek, that simply said 'welcome' and then immediately pivoted to a fox update. They will learn. We all learned. The chat does not change for anyone.

The neighbourhood group chat has a member who responds to every single post, no matter how minor, with a single thumbs-up emoji. A lost cat: thumbs up. A burst water main: thumbs up. A heartfelt message about a resident moving away: thumbs up. We do not know who they are. We do not know what the thumb means. But it arrives, always, within minutes, a small reliable gesture from the void, and honestly, in these uncertain times, I have come to find the thumb comforting.

A man posted in the neighbourhood group chat to complain that a different man's hedge was 'getting out of hand'. The accused hedge-owner replied. The original man replied to the reply. Photographs of the hedge were submitted as evidence, from multiple angles, in different lighting. The hedge dispute now has its own lore, its own factions, its own grim history. The hedge itself, I should note, looks completely fine. It is, by any measure, just a hedge.

Somebody posted in the chat, late at night, the single word 'BANG??'. Just that. Two letters of question. The chat exploded. Forty replies in twenty minutes, everyone awake now, everyone alarmed, everyone reporting their own bangs from over the years. And then, at midnight, the original poster returned and wrote, casually, 'sorry all, was my bin lid'. The chat went silent. We had bonded over nothing. We had been a community, for one beautiful hour, because of a bin lid.

The neighbourhood group chat held a vote on a proposed change to the bin collection day, and that vote split the community into two bitter, irreconcilable camps. There were essays. There were veiled insults. There was a man who left the chat dramatically, only to rejoin eleven minutes later, unable to stay away. The bins are, ultimately, collected by the council, on a schedule the council decides. None of our voting mattered. But we had, for a week, a war, and the war was ours.

A resident posted a long, heartfelt, beautifully written message in the neighbourhood group chat thanking the community for their kindness during a difficult time. It was genuinely moving. Several people were touched. And then, directly beneath it, with no acknowledgement whatsoever, Derek posted a photograph of the fox standing near a recycling box, captioned 'he's back'. The fox does not respect the moment. Derek does not respect the moment. The chat moves only forward.

I watched a chef on television debone a fish in eleven seconds with a single fluid, balletic motion, and I thought, with the unearned confidence of a man on a sofa, 'I could do that'. I could not do that. I have just spent forty minutes attacking a fish with a knife, and the fish has, somehow, won. There is fish in places fish should not be. The kitchen looks like a crime scene. The chef on television is a trained professional. I am a man who watched a man.

The cooking show host casually 'flipped' the contents of the pan with a confident flick of the wrist, sending the food up in a graceful arc and catching it perfectly. I tried this. I sent a quantity of stir-fried vegetables directly upwards. Some of them returned to the pan. Most of them did not. Some of them, I believe, are still on the ceiling, in a pattern, like a small green constellation, a permanent monument to my belief in myself.

The recipe on the cooking show was described, repeatedly, as 'a simple midweek supper'. The host, smiling, called it 'fuss-free'. The 'simple, fuss-free midweek supper' required four pans, three hours, a cut of meat I had to order specially, and a technique called 'reducing' that I now understand to be a euphemism for 'standing at the stove watching a liquid for a very long time'. It is Wednesday. It is 10 p.m. I have not yet eaten. The supper has fussed.

On the cooking show, the host always has a small bowl of every ingredient, pre-measured, pre-chopped, lined up in a beautiful row, ready to go. They call this 'mise en place'. They do not show you who chopped all of those things. They do not show you the forty minutes of weeping over onions. The bowls simply exist, perfect and prepared, and I, watching, believed that cooking was the easy part, the part with the bowls. It is not. The bowls are everything. The bowls are a lie.

The host of the cooking show said, with a relaxed smile, 'and now we just let it rest'. I had never heard food described as needing rest. But I trusted the show, and so my roast chicken rested. It rested for the recommended time. And then, full of confidence, I carved it and served it, and it was, to be fair to the chicken, perfectly fine. The chicken had rested. I, who had cleaned three pans and wept over garlic, had not. There is no segment for the cook's rest.

Every cooking show host, at some point, tastes their own creation, closes their eyes, and makes a small noise of private ecstasy. I have started doing this. I made a perfectly ordinary pasta last night, tasted it, closed my eyes, and made the noise. My flatmate was watching. There was a silence. The pasta did not warrant the noise. The pasta was a four out of ten. But the show told me to make the noise, and so I make the noise, and my flatmate is, I think, concerned.

The cooking show host said, breezily, 'don't worry about being precise, cooking is all about feeling'. I took this advice into my kitchen. I did not measure. I cooked by feeling. I felt my way through an entire curry. And the curry, the curry that I felt, was a disaster, an inedible monument to vibes. It turns out that 'cooking is all about feeling' is something only said by people who have spent twenty years learning, very precisely, exactly how much of everything to use.

I watched a baking show and decided that I, too, would 'just whip up' a batch of pastry from scratch, because the contestants made it look like a light, breezy, fifteen-minute affair. The pastry I produced was tough enough to resole a boot. It turns out 'whipping up' pastry is a skill honed over years, and the contestants on the show, who I had assumed were ordinary people, are in fact wizards, and I had watched a wizardry programme and thought it was a tutorial.

The cooking show host produced a 'quick stock' by, apparently, simmering some bones for what they implied was a short, casual moment. I made my own stock. It took the entire day. The kitchen smelled, for hours, of a soup that did not yet exist. By the time the stock was ready it was dark outside, I had missed two phone calls, and I had a single jar of brown liquid that the host could buy, in a carton, for ninety pence. But mine, I tell myself, has soul. Mine has cost me a Saturday.

The host on the cooking show kept saying that a particular technique was 'foolproof'. I am, it turns out, a more advanced category of fool than the technique was prepared for. I followed every step. I followed them in order. And yet the foolproof dish, the dish that could not be ruined, lies before me, ruined, smoking gently, and I have proven, through dedicated effort, that there exists no proof against a fool of sufficient commitment.

I have just collected my new passport photos, and the person looking back at me from these images is not a person I recognise or particularly want to be associated with for the next ten years. I am not allowed to smile. I am not allowed to look happy. The official guidance demands a 'neutral expression', and so I appear, in all four photos, like a man who has just been gravely insulted and is choosing, with great difficulty, not to react.

The passport photo booth is a small fabric cubicle of judgement. You sit on a stool that cannot be adjusted to any human height. A disembodied voice tells you to look at the camera. A green light promises a photo, then a flash arrives several seconds later, capturing not your prepared face but your true face, the face of a person waiting, uncertain, slightly afraid. That face is now my legal identity. That face will be scrutinised by border officials worldwide.

My old passport photo, taken ten years ago, shows a young, hopeful, well-rested individual with a full head of dark hair and a face untouched by mortgages. My new passport photo shows the same person, after the decade happened to him. Holding the two side by side is like watching a time-lapse of a slow surrender. The border official will glance from the photo to me and back, and in that glance will be the entire story of what life does to a man.

I tried to take my own passport photo at home to save money, against a white wall, holding my phone at arm's length. I took, in total, eighty-four photographs. In every single one, I am either blinking, leaning, smiling slightly, casting a shadow, or wearing an expression that the official website firmly describes as 'not acceptable'. I have, somehow, never seen my own face look correct. I went to the booth. The booth captured my wrongness in one efficient flash.

The rules for the passport photo are extensive and unforgiving. No glasses. No hats. No hair across the face. No shadows. No red-eye. Mouth closed. Eyes open. Neutral expression. By the time I had satisfied every single requirement, I had been so thoroughly stripped of all personality, all warmth, all spark of the living, that the photograph that emerged was less a portrait and more a missing-person poster issued in advance.

There is a strange cruelty in the fact that the passport photo, the single official image of you presented to the world, the one used to confirm that you are a real and respectable human being, is also the worst photograph of you that exists. I have wedding photos. I have holiday photos. None of these are in my passport. In my passport is a startled criminal, and that startled criminal is who every country I visit will believe me to be.

I showed my new passport photo to my partner, hoping for reassurance. My partner looked at it for a long moment, looked at me, looked at the photo again, and then said, carefully, the way one speaks to someone about to receive difficult news, 'it really captures you'. This was not the comfort I sought. This was a verdict. I have placed the passport in a drawer and I do not intend to look at it again until I am forced to, at an airport, in front of strangers.

The booth printed my four photographs and I examined them in the harsh light outside, hoping that perhaps one of the four would be acceptable, would be the one good one. They are identical. Of course they are identical. They were taken half a second apart. But I keep examining them, as if photo three might, on closer inspection, reveal a hidden charm, a secret dignity, that photos one, two, and four lack. They will not. They are four windows onto the same small disaster.

I have decided that the unflattering passport photo is, in fact, a clever security feature. No criminal could ever successfully impersonate me, because no criminal would willingly choose to look like the man in my passport. The photo is so deeply, profoundly unappealing that it functions, on its own, as a deterrent. My identity is protected not by technology but by the sheer, off-putting strangeness of my own official face.

The photographer at the chemist's took one look at my first attempt and said, gently, 'your ears need to be visible'. I have, apparently, been hiding my ears. I did not know I had been hiding my ears. I tucked my hair back, exposing two ears I had not consciously thought about in years, and the photographer nodded with satisfaction. My passport is now, primarily, a document about my ears. The face is incidental. The ears are the point.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: I was nominated to take the group photo at the family gathering, which meant that for the next fifteen minutes I held a phone aloft, shouting increasingly desperate instructions at eleven relatives who would not stop moving. 'Squeeze in. Squeeze in more. Uncle Pete, you're gone, come back. The baby's facing the wrong way. Someone's eyes are shut.' I took forty photographs. In every single one, a different person is ruining it. Mathematically, the perfect photo may not exist.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: We asked a kind passing stranger to take a photo of our whole group in front of the famous landmark. The stranger, full of goodwill, took the phone, stepped back, and then took eleven photographs of, primarily, our knees. The landmark is not in any of them. Half the group is not in any of them. But we thanked the stranger warmly, because they had tried, and you cannot tell a kind stranger that they have photographed your knees. You simply keep the knee photos. Forever.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: The phone was propped against a water bottle, the timer was set, and I had ten seconds to sprint from the camera into position with the rest of the group. I have done this before. I know the run. But the timer is always faster than a human being, and the resulting photograph captures the group, smiling serenely, and me, a blur at the edge of the frame, mid-leap, my face a mask of pure athletic panic, arriving at the photo a fraction of a second too late.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: Taking a group photo requires every single member of the group to blink in unison, between photographs, and never during one. This is, statistically, almost impossible with a group of eight. There is always one. There is always, in the otherwise perfect photo, one person with their eyes serenely closed, looking peaceful, looking asleep, having chosen, of all the available moments, that exact thousandth of a second to rest their eyes. We have a photo album full of one sleeping relative at a time.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: I suggested we take a 'natural, candid' group photo, where everyone is just laughing and being themselves, rather than a stiff posed one. So I told everyone to 'just laugh naturally'. Nobody can laugh naturally on command. The resulting photograph shows nine people performing the physical act of laughter while their eyes contain nothing but fear and confusion. It is the least natural image ever captured. We look like a group of strangers being held against our will.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: There is always one tall person and one short person in a group photo, and arranging them is a feat of military planning. The tall one is sent to the back, where they loom. The short one is brought to the front, where they are partially obscured by the people next to them. We rearrange. We reconsider. We build, essentially, a small human pyramid, and after eight minutes of architecture, we capture a photo in which the short person is, somehow, still hidden behind an elbow.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: After taking the group photo, I made the fatal error of saying 'let me just check it'. This is the sentence that ends an afternoon. Because once I check it, I will find a flaw, and once I find a flaw, we must take it again, and again, and the group, who thought they were free, who had begun to relax, must reassemble, must re-squeeze, must summon the smile once more, and they will all, quietly, begin to hate me, the photographer, the perfectionist, the captor.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: We took the group photo with my phone, and then a chorus rose up: 'take one on mine too'. And so I took it on the next phone. And the next. And the next. I have now photographed the same eight people, in the same pose, eleven times, on eleven devices, and the eight people have held the smile across all eleven, the smile slowly dying, becoming a grimace, becoming a plea. The photo exists eleven times now. It exists too many times. It is everywhere.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: The group photo was finally, miraculously, perfect. Everyone's eyes were open. Everyone was smiling genuinely. The lighting was kind. The landmark was visible. It was the one. And then, in the bottom corner of the frame, I noticed a complete stranger, a man eating an ice cream, looking directly into the lens with an expression of total calm. He has joined our family photo forever. We do not know him. He is, now, a permanent member of our holiday, and honestly, he photographs better than several of us.

subtopic: trying to take a group photo
sentence: The group photo descended into chaos when someone suggested 'a silly one'. We had a perfectly good serious photo. But the silly one had been suggested, and so we had to do the silly one, and the silly one involved everyone pulling a face and one person attempting a small jump. The silly photo took eleven attempts, far more than the serious photo, because being silly on demand is exhausting, and by the end the silliness had curdled into a kind of grim, committed despair.

My hairdresser asked, as they always do, 'so, are you going anywhere nice on your holidays?'. I am not going anywhere. I have no holidays planned. But I cannot say this, because that would create a small, sad silence in the salon, and so I invented, on the spot, a trip to Portugal. I now have a fictional holiday in Portugal that I must remember the details of, because my hairdresser will, in six weeks, ask me how Portugal was.

There is a specific peril in the hairdresser's chair, which is that you are facing a large mirror, watching yourself being spoken to, and you must respond to the conversation while also pretending not to be staring directly at your own slowly-emerging haircut.
