I do not know where to look. If I look at the hairdresser, I have to twist my head, which they dislike. If I look at the mirror, I am looking at myself, vainly. I have settled, throughout, on looking at a poster about conditioner.

The hairdresser held up the small mirror behind my head, to show me the back of my own haircut, a part of myself I have never once seen in real life and cannot meaningfully evaluate. I looked into the mirror at the reflection of a mirror, at a region of my own head, and I had no opinion, no frame of reference, no idea what 'good' would even look like back there. So I said, as I always say, with great false confidence, 'yeah, lovely, perfect'.

I went to the hairdresser and, when asked what I wanted, I gestured vaguely at my own head and said 'just, you know, a tidy-up, neaten it'. This is not instruction. This is not information. I have given the hairdresser nothing, a void, a shrug, and now they must guess, must read my soul, must intuit from my general energy what a person like me deserves. They did their best. The result is fine. It is always fine. 'Fine' is the natural outcome of communicating with a shrug.

My hairdresser and I have, over six years and many appointments, built a relationship of remarkable depth, in which we know almost nothing about each other. I know they have a sister. They know I 'work with computers'. We discuss the weather, the traffic, and a television programme we are both vaguely aware of. We are not friends. We could not pick each other out of a crowd outside the salon. But for forty minutes, every two months, we are the closest of confidants, and then we are strangers again.

The hairdresser asked me, mid-cut, 'and what do you do for work?'. I have a job that is genuinely difficult to explain, involving spreadsheets and a sector nobody understands, and so I said, as I always do, 'oh, it's boring, office stuff'. The hairdresser nodded kindly, accepting this. I have now described my entire professional identity, the thing I do for forty hours a week, as 'office stuff', and I felt, briefly, the deep peace of being fully unknowable.

There is a difficult moment, near the end of the haircut, when the conversation has run its natural course. We have done the holidays. We have done the weather. We have done the weekend. And there is still ten minutes of cutting left, ten minutes of silence to fill, and we both feel it arriving, the conversational drought, and we both reach, desperately, for a new topic, and one of us says, 'busy in here today?', and we are saved, for now.

My hairdresser asked if I had 'any big plans for the weekend'. I did not. My big plan for the weekend was to do some laundry and possibly tidy a cupboard. I could not say this. So I said, 'oh, just seeing some friends, the usual', which implied a rich and active social life I do not possess. The hairdresser smiled, pleased for me. I have now lied, again, in this chair, and the lies are accumulating, an entire false biography assembled forty minutes at a time.

The hairdresser, near the end, picked up a small can and asked, 'do you want some product in it?'. I never know what to say to this. I do not know what 'product' is. I do not know what it does. I have a vision of leaving the salon, getting rained on, and the product running down my face like a melting candle. But saying no feels like a rejection, like declining a gift, and so I said yes, and now my hair is crunchy, and I am afraid to touch it.

I switched to a new hairdresser, a betrayal I committed quietly and have never confessed. But my old neighbourhood is small, and I now live in fear of being seen by my old hairdresser, of being spotted on the street with a haircut they did not give me, a haircut performed by another's hands. They would know. They would see, instantly, the work of a rival. I take the long way round now. I avoid that street. The guilt of the haircut affair follows me everywhere.

I tried to text my boss 'I'll be there shortly' and my phone, in its infinite confidence, changed 'shortly' to 'shorty'. I did not notice. I sent it. I have now addressed my line manager, a serious woman in her fifties, as 'shorty', and informed her that I will be arriving as such. She has not replied. The message sits there, delivered, read, unanswered. I have considered changing my name and moving abroad. Autocorrect did this. Autocorrect, and my own failure to look.

My phone has decided, with no consultation, that whenever I type the perfectly common word 'well', I actually mean 'we'll'. I do not. I rarely mean 'we'll'. But my phone has fallen in love with that apostrophe and inserts it everywhere, and so my messages now contain sentences like 'I'm not feeling we'll today', which makes me sound less like a tired person and more like a poorly translated philosophy. I have corrected it a thousand times. The phone does not learn. The phone believes.

I was texting a friend about meeting for dinner and my phone changed 'see you at six' to 'see you at sox'. My friend, a literal person, replied 'where is sox?'. I do not know where sox is. Sox is not a place. But for a glorious confused half-hour, we both operated as though sox might be a venue, a bar, a small establishment we had simply forgotten the existence of. We met, eventually, at six. We never found sox. Sox haunts me still.

I attempted to send my mother a warm and loving birthday message. I typed 'Happy birthday, hope you have a lovely day'. My phone, however, transformed 'lovely' into 'lonely', and so my mother received, on the morning of her birthday, from her only child, the message 'hope you have a lonely day'. She phoned me. There was hurt in her voice. It took eleven minutes to explain the technology. The technology had, in eleven characters, undone a year of being a good son.

There is a particular cruelty in the way autocorrect waits. It behaves perfectly for ordinary, low-stakes messages. It only reveals its true chaotic nature in important messages, formal messages, messages to people you wish to impress. I wrote a careful, professional email on my phone, and autocorrect, silent until that moment, chose to change one crucial word into something unrepeatable. It had been waiting. It had been watching. It struck when the stakes were highest, like a small linguistic assassin.

My phone refuses to learn the name of my friend Siobhan. I have typed it correctly hundreds of times. The phone changes it, every time, to a different word entirely, a word that is not a name, a word that has no business being there. Siobhan now appears in my messages as 'shoehorn', as 'show ban', as a string of suggestions that grow, frankly, more insulting over time. Siobhan has seen this. Siobhan is no longer entirely sure how I feel about her.

I sent a quick message in the family group chat and noticed, too late, the moment after sending, that autocorrect had inserted a baffling, surreal phrase into the middle of an ordinary sentence. There is no 'undo'. There is no recall. The message is out, in the world, being read by aunts. And so I did what we all do: I sent a follow-up message saying '*' and the correct word, and trusted that an asterisk and a single word would somehow heal the wound. It does not. It never does.

Autocorrect has a special, dedicated hatred for the word 'definitely'. It will not allow it. Every time I attempt to type 'definitely', confidently, into a message, the phone wrestles me for control and produces, instead, 'defiantly'. And so I have, over the years, told a great many people that I will 'defiantly be there', that I 'defiantly agree', that something is 'defiantly the best option'. I sound, in all my messages, like a man entering every situation ready for a fight.

I have started, out of sheer self-defence, reading every message four times before sending it, scanning each one like a bomb disposal expert searching for autocorrect's hidden work. And still things get through. Last week, despite my vigilance, despite four full readings, I sent a colleague a message that I am certain I typed correctly, and which arrived containing a word neither of us had ever seen before. We have not discussed it. We are pretending it did not happen. This is the modern condition.

My phone now suggests entire words and phrases before I have typed them, predicting what I want to say, finishing my sentences for me, and it is, frankly, unsettling how often it is correct. It knows me. It has read enough of my messages to anticipate my dull, predictable thoughts. But occasionally it predicts something strange, something I would never say, and I am left wondering: is the phone wrong, or does the phone know a version of me I have not yet met?

There is a man in the gym locker room who conducts his entire post-workout routine in a state of complete, confident nudity, towel slung casually over his shoulder rather than deployed in any useful capacity. He chats. He browses his phone. He discusses, at length, the football. The rest of us perform a careful, fully-clothed ballet of avoidance, changing at impossible angles, while he stands among us, serene, free, a man entirely at peace with himself, and with everyone else's discomfort.

I have forgotten my padlock combination. I am standing in front of my own locker, in the gym, in my coat, with all my belongings sealed inside, and the four numbers that would free them have simply left my mind. I try combinations. I try my birthday. I try the year. The locker, indifferent, holds firm. I will have to find a member of staff and explain, with great shame, that I have been defeated by a small lock that I myself set, this morning, with my own hands.

The gym locker room has a set of scales, positioned in a high-traffic area, and stepping onto them is the single bravest act available to a gym-goer. To weigh yourself, in public, where others might glance over and see the number, is to expose your soul. I have developed a technique of stepping on, glancing down for a fraction of a second, registering the number through pure peripheral vision, and stepping off, all in under two seconds, like a man defusing his own self-esteem.

I always choose the locker furthest from anyone else, in the quietest corner, claiming my small territory. And without fail, the very next person to enter the entire empty locker room will walk directly to the locker immediately beside mine, out of all the available lockers, and begin to change, and now we are two strangers in close proximity in a vast empty room, and neither of us will ever acknowledge how strange this is, and neither of us will move.

The hand dryer in the gym locker room is so powerful that it does not merely dry your hands, it reshapes them, sending the skin rippling in waves, revealing in vivid detail every vein and tendon you possess. I use it because it is there, and I watch, transfixed and slightly alarmed, as my own hands are transformed into a moving anatomical diagram. It is, I think, the most exciting forty seconds of my visit, which says something troubling about the workout I have just completed.

There is an unspoken rule in the gym locker room that one does not make eye contact, does not speak, and certainly does not initiate conversation. It is a place of silent, focused changing. And so, of course, there is always one cheerful, friendly soul who has not received this memo, who greets everyone, who comments on the weather, who asks how your workout was, and who is met, every time, with the polite, terrified, monosyllabic responses of people whose social contract he has shattered.

I packed my gym bag this morning with great care and arrived at the locker room to discover that I had brought everything except a towel. I have a towel at home. I have several towels. None of them are here. I now face a difficult negotiation with the day: do I skip the shower, and travel home unwashed, or do I attempt to dry myself, post-shower, using only a t-shirt and willpower. I have done both, in my time. Neither path leads anywhere good.

The gym locker room benches are exactly the wrong width, too narrow to comfortably sit on, too wide to easily reach over. Every person in the room is engaged in the same awkward struggle: balancing precariously on the edge of a bench while attempting to put on a sock, a task that requires standing on one leg, which the bench actively prevents. We hop. We wobble. We grab at lockers for support. The locker room is, daily, a small uncoordinated festival of grown adults losing their balance.

I left my gym bag on the locker room bench for ninety seconds while I filled my water bottle, and returned to find that the entire room had silently rearranged itself around it. New people had arrived. They had changed around my abandoned bag, treating it with the careful respect of a small monument, nobody touching it, nobody moving it, everyone simply working around the mysterious unattended bag, and I felt, retrieving it, that I had inconvenienced an entire community.

There is a specific category of gym-goer who arrives, opens their locker, sets up an elaborate base camp of toiletries, supplements, and equipment, and then proceeds to spend significantly more time in the locker room than they ever spend in the actual gym. I have watched a man arrange his shelf of products for eleven minutes. I do not know if he ever exercises. I think, for him, the gym is the locker room, and the locker room is a hobby, and the weights are merely an excuse.

The map app, in a voice of total serene confidence, instructed me to 'turn right'. There was no right. There was a wall. There was a canal. There was, in the direction the app insisted I turn, nothing a car could possibly do except enter the water. I did not turn right. The app, undeterred, immediately announced it was 'recalculating', in a tone that contained, I am certain, a note of disappointment, as though I, and not the canal, were the problem.

I have a complicated relationship with the map app's estimated arrival time. It tells me I will arrive at 3:14, with the precision of a prophet, and I structure my entire emotional state around that number. And then traffic happens, and the number creeps to 3:22, to 3:31, to 3:48, and I watch my promised future slowly dissolve, minute by minute, and I feel each lost minute personally, as a small bereavement, as a thing the app had given me and then cruelly taken back.

The map app guided me, with great confidence, off the sensible main road and into a labyrinth of narrow country lanes, each one barely wider than the car, each one bordered by towering hedges, in the name of saving, the app promised, four minutes. I did not save four minutes. I met a tractor. There was a reversing situation that lasted, itself, six minutes. The app does not factor in tractors. The app lives in a world without tractors, a smooth digital world, and it has never had to look one in the eye.

The map app told me my destination was 'on the right'. I slowed down. I looked right. There was nothing on the right that resembled my destination. There was a hedge, a postbox, and a field of sheep. The app, however, was certain, and announced cheerfully, 'you have arrived'. I have not arrived. I am parked beside some sheep. The sheep are looking at me. The app considers its job complete, and has, in fact, already stopped giving directions, leaving me alone, with the sheep, nowhere.

The map app delivers its instructions with such a slight delay that 'turn left' arrives at the precise moment the left turn becomes physically impossible. I sail past the junction. The app says 'recalculating'. We do this dance at every turn. I have begun to suspect the app enjoys it, that the delay is not a flaw but a feature, a small game it plays, watching me sail past turning after turning, gently, patiently, recalculating my failures for the entire length of the journey.

My passenger, an old-fashioned soul, brought a paper map. I scoffed. I had the app. The app knew everything. And then, deep in a valley, the phone signal vanished, and the app's confident blue dot froze, stranded, lost, blinking helplessly in a grey void. And my passenger, calm, unhurried, unfolded the paper map across her knees, found us with one finger, and navigated us out by the ancient art of looking at where things actually were. I have not scoffed since.

The map app offered me three routes to the same place: one labelled 'fastest', one 'shortest', and one labelled, mysteriously, simply with a small icon and no explanation. I chose the unexplained one, out of curiosity, a fatal flaw of mine. It took me through an industrial estate, past a sewage works, over a level crossing, and along a road being actively resurfaced. It was not faster. It was not shorter. It was, the app seemed to believe, character-building, and I suppose, on reflection, it was.

The map app told me to take 'the second exit' at the roundabout. But the roundabout had a confusing fifth exit that may or may not have been a real road, and a slip road that complicated the entire count, and so the question of which exit was truly 'the second' became a philosophical one, a matter of interpretation, of judgement. I chose. I chose wrong. I went round again. I have now circled this roundabout three times, like a man trapped in a small concrete poem about indecision.

I asked the map app for walking directions in an unfamiliar city, and it immediately spun me on the spot, demanding I 'head north'. I do not know where north is. North is not a direction available to my body. I held the phone flat, I turned slowly in a full circle, watching the little arrow swing wildly, while a street full of people watched me, a lost man, performing a slow, confused pirouette on the pavement, in search of a north that, frankly, I have never once located in my life.

The map app routed me, with total confidence, directly into the centre of a town on market day, a town whose narrow medieval streets had not been designed with the motor car, or indeed with the app, in mind. The blue line on my screen sailed smoothly through stalls, pedestrians, and a brass band. The app saw no obstacle. The app saw a clear road. I, however, saw a town crier, and a man selling cheese, and absolutely nowhere to go.

The office printer has displayed the message 'paper jam' for so long that we have begun to question whether there is, in fact, any paper, or any jam, or whether the printer has simply chosen this phrase as a permanent personality. I have opened every tray. I have examined every roller. There is no jam. The printer remains insistent. I believe, increasingly, that 'paper jam' is the printer's way of expressing a deeper, more existential complaint that it cannot put into other words.

I sent one single document to the office printer, a single page, and the printer responded by demanding I install a driver, update the firmware, log into an account I did not know I had, and confirm, repeatedly, that I genuinely wished to print. By the time the page emerged, twenty minutes later, I had forgotten what the document was, why I needed it, and, briefly, who I was. The printer had won, as the printer always wins.

There is one person in the office who knows how to fix the printer, and that person has, through this single skill, become the most powerful individual in the building. When the printer breaks, we do not call IT. We seek out Margaret. We bring Margaret offerings. We speak to Margaret kindly all year, banking goodwill, because we know that one day the printer will jam and only Margaret can save us, and Margaret knows it too.

The office printer can sense urgency. On an ordinary, calm afternoon, it will print whatever you like, smoothly, without complaint. But the moment you need forty copies of a document for a meeting that begins in nine minutes, the printer detects your panic, draws strength from it, and immediately runs out of toner, jams two trays, and displays an error code that does not appear in any manual on earth. The printer feeds on deadlines. It always has.

I went to collect my printout and found, in the output tray, forty-one pages belonging to a colleague, a colleague who had sent them to print and then, apparently, simply forgotten, abandoning them to the world. I now know things about that colleague's work, and possibly their personal life, that I was never meant to know. The office printer is not a printer. The office printer is a confessional, and nobody collects their sins.

Every printout that emerges from the office printer carries, somewhere on the page, a faint grey streak, a ghostly vertical line, a small permanent flaw. We have all noticed it. Nobody has fixed it. We have collectively decided that the streak is fine, that it is, in fact, simply a feature of all documents now, and that any document arriving without the streak would, frankly, look suspicious, look fake, look like it came from somewhere better than here.

I approached the office printer to retrieve a document and found three colleagues already gathered around it, each waiting for their own printout, none of them speaking, all of them watching the printer with the quiet, patient hope of people at a fishing spot. We stood together in silence. The printer worked through its queue at its own unhurried pace. It was, in its way, a moment of communion, four office workers united by the slow, sacred ritual of waiting for paper.

The office printer asked me, via a small screen, to 'replace toner cartridge'. I did not know where the toner cartridge lived, what it looked like, or whether I was authorised to touch it. I opened a panel. Inside was a complex landscape of components, none labelled, none welcoming. I closed the panel. I have decided that the toner is not my responsibility, that it belongs to a larger system, to society, to someone braver, and I have walked away, and the printer's screen still glows accusingly behind me.

I pressed print, and nothing happened. I pressed print again. Still nothing. I pressed print eleven times, in mounting frustration, and then went to investigate the printer, and discovered, of course, what I always discover, which is that the printer was offline, and that it had silently accepted all eleven of my commands, and that the moment I brought it back online it would, with great enthusiasm, print eleven copies of everything, and I would have to explain the eleven copies to Margaret.

The office got a new printer, a sleek, modern, expensive machine that the email announcing it described as 'intuitive' and 'effortless'. The new printer is neither of these things. The new printer has a touchscreen with forty options, a menu structure of baffling depth, and a habit of logging you out mid-task. We all miss the old printer now. The old printer jammed constantly, yes, but the old printer was ours, and we understood its sorrows, and it understood ours.

The website informed me that my password must contain an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number, a special character, and, presumably, a small piece of my soul. I constructed something that satisfied all of these demands, a password of such complexity that no human, including me, could ever hope to recall it. It is now lost. It guards my account from intruders, and also, perfectly, from me. The account and I will never meet again.

I clicked 'forgot password', as I do, weekly, with the weary familiarity of a man visiting an old friend. The website sent me a link. The link asked me to create a new password. The website then informed me, with a small note of disapproval, that my new password 'cannot be the same as a previous password'. It knew. It remembered. The website remembers every password I have ever had, perfectly, forever, which is, frankly, more than I can say for myself.

My entire digital life is protected by a system of passwords that are, in truth, all small variations of the same password, with a number on the end that increases by one each time I am forced to change it. I am currently on the seventh iteration. A hacker who guessed the base word would, with eight quick attempts, own everything I have ever cared about. But it has a capital letter and an exclamation mark, and so the website considers it 'strong', and I, too, have chosen to believe.

I was finally persuaded to use a password manager, a single app to hold all my passwords safely behind one master password. This is a brilliant, sensible system, and I have ruined it, because I have forgotten the master password. All my passwords are now locked, perfectly secure, inside a vault I cannot open, and the key to the vault is somewhere in my memory, in a room I cannot find, and I have, through the pursuit of good security, locked myself entirely out of my own existence.

The login screen offered me a choice: enter my password, or answer a 'security question'. The security question was 'what was the name of your first pet?'. I have, in my life, given several different answers to this question across several different websites, in several different moods, and I no longer know which lie I told where. My first pet has, through my own carelessness, acquired four names, and any of them might be the truth, and the website is waiting.

I typed my password, confidently, and the website rejected it. I typed it again, more carefully, certain I had simply mistyped. Rejected. I typed it a third time, slowly, deliberately, treating each character as precious. Rejected. And then came the cold, creeping horror, the realisation that the password in my head, the password I trusted, the password I have used for years, is simply, somehow, no longer the password, and I do not know when it stopped being the password, or what it is now.

The website made me change my password and then, immediately, on the very next screen, asked me to log in again using my new password, the password I had created eleven seconds earlier and had already, in those eleven seconds, completely forgotten. I sat there, staring, my mind a clean white void. The password was new. The password was gone. The website and I, both of us, waited for a memory that was never coming back.

I keep my passwords written down, all of them, on a small piece of paper, in a drawer, which every expert agrees is the worst possible thing a person can do. But the experts have not met my memory. The experts trust me to remember forty unique strings of nonsense. The experts are dreamers. The little piece of paper, hidden among the spare keys and dead batteries, is the only thing standing between me and total digital exile, and I love it.

The password field showed my password as a row of small dots, hiding it for my own protection, in case a spy was reading over my shoulder. There was no spy. There is never a spy. I am alone, in my kitchen, at night. But the website does not know this, and so it hides my password from me, the one person who is desperately, urgently trying to see it, while protecting it from a watcher who does not, and has never, existed.

I logged into an account I had not visited in three years, and the password came to me instantly, perfectly, with no effort at all, a password I did not know I still knew. And yet the password I set last Tuesday, the recent one, the important one, has vanished. My memory has decided, on its own, which passwords matter, and it is wrong about all of them, and there is nothing, apparently, that I can do to correct its strange and useless filing system.

I have started talking to my houseplants, partly because an article said it helps them grow, and partly because the houseplants, unlike most of the people in my life, never interrupt, never disagree, and never bring up that thing I said at a party in 2019. I tell them about my day. They listen, in their leafy way. It is the most balanced and supportive relationship I currently have, and I am only slightly concerned about what that says.

I read that plants respond well to encouragement, and so I now deliver a small daily motivational speech to my fern. I tell it that it is doing wonderfully. I tell it that I believe in it. I tell it that the new leaf is its finest work yet. The fern, to be fair, is thriving, although whether this is due to my speeches or the simple application of water remains, scientifically, an open question that I am not willing to test, in case the answer hurts the fern's feelings.

My partner walked into the room and found me leaning over the spider plant, speaking to it in a low, gentle, confiding voice. There was a pause. My partner did not ask what I was doing. My partner simply nodded, slowly, the way one nods at a development one had long suspected was coming, and quietly left the room, and the spider plant and I returned to our conversation, which was, for the record, about the weather.

I have given each of my plants a distinct personality, and I greet them accordingly each morning. The cheese plant is greeted with respect, because the cheese plant has earned it. The basil is greeted with anxious encouragement, because the basil is always, somehow, on the brink. The cactus is greeted with a simple nod, because the cactus is a professional and does not require small talk. I run, essentially, a small office, and the plants are my staff, and morale is high.

When a plant of mine begins to droop, I do not immediately reach for water or fertiliser. First, I have a word with it. I ask it, gently, what is wrong. I wait, as though a leafy green creature might, given time and a safe space, articulate its needs. The plant never answers. The plant cannot answer. But I feel that the conversation has been had, that the plant has been heard, and then I water it, which was, of course, the actual solution all along.

I went away for a week and asked a friend to water my plants, and I left her a note. The note, I realised later, addressed each plant by name and included small personal instructions, such as 'Geraldine likes to be misted, but do not overdo it, she finds it overwhelming'. My friend watered the plants. My friend also, I am fairly sure, photographed the note, and I am fairly sure the note has now been seen by people I will have to face at social events.

I caught myself apologising to a plant. I had knocked it slightly while reaching for a book, a leaf had bent, and the words 'oh, sorry' left my mouth before any conscious thought could stop them. The plant accepted the apology with the silent grace plants always show. And I stood there, in my own living room, having just apologised, sincerely, to a pot of greenery, and I understood that some line had been crossed, some time ago, and that I was not going to be coming back.

My new plant has not yet been spoken to, because I have not yet decided what sort of voice it has, what sort of personality lives inside it. This is an important decision and it cannot be rushed. The other plants all have established characters, established relationships with me, and the new arrival must be properly understood before it can join the conversation. It sits on the windowsill, silent, unnamed, in a kind of probationary period, and I observe it, and I wait for it to reveal itself.

I told a friend, lightly, as a joke, that I talk to my plants, expecting her to laugh. She did not laugh. She told me, in complete seriousness, that she does the same, that she has done it for years, that her monstera is called Clive and that Clive is, in her words, 'a good listener'. And in that moment a great wall fell between us, and we recognised one another, two members of the same quiet, slightly unhinged society, and our friendship deepened immeasurably.

One of my plants died, despite my speeches, despite my encouragement, despite a relationship I had genuinely come to value. And I found, to my own surprise, that I delivered a short eulogy, standing over the compost bin, a few quiet words about a fern that had tried its best. My partner observed this from the doorway and said nothing, only later, gently, asked whether I might like to 'do something this weekend that involves other humans', and I conceded that this was, perhaps, fair.

My alarm goes off, and in the warm dark I make a series of solemn, urgent promises to myself: I will get up after just one more snooze. Just one. This is the deal. And then the snooze ends, and the past version of me who made that deal is gone, vanished, unreachable, and a new version of me, who never agreed to anything, presses the button again, and so it goes, a relay of liars, each one betraying the next, until the morning is half gone.

I have calculated that the nine minutes the snooze button grants me are not, in any meaningful sense, rest. They are nine minutes of shallow, anxious, dread-soaked half-sleep, during which my brain runs a constant background process reminding me that the alarm is coming back. It is not sleep. It is a small, recurring waiting room. And yet I return to it, again and again, because the alternative is standing up, and standing up is unthinkable.

In a moment of bold strategic thinking, I moved my alarm clock across the room, so that I would be forced to physically get out of bed to silence it. This was meant to defeat the snooze button forever. Instead, I have simply learned to cross the room, switch off the alarm, and return to bed, all while remaining, essentially, asleep. I have evolved. The strategy has been defeated. The bed always wins. The bed has been doing this for much longer than I have.

Every night, full of optimism, I set my alarm for the time a productive, admirable person would rise. I picture that person: calm, unhurried, sipping coffee, watching the sunrise. And every morning, that admirable person is nowhere to be found, replaced by the actual me, who negotiates with the snooze button for forty minutes and then begins the day in a state of pure, sprinting panic. The two of us, the planner and the sleeper, have never once met.

I have tried alarm apps designed to defeat the snooze button: apps that make you solve a maths problem, scan a barcode in the bathroom, or shake the phone forty times. I have defeated all of them. I can solve a complex maths problem while fully asleep, it turns out, and then go back to bed, and remember none of it. My brain, lazy and useless all day, becomes a genius the instant there is a chance of more sleep on the line.

There is a specific, beautiful, doomed moment, perhaps four snoozes deep, when I open one eye, look at the time, and perform a desperate piece of mental arithmetic: if I skip breakfast, and skip the shower, and run, I can still snooze once more. The maths is always wrong. The maths is always optimistic. But I do the maths anyway, every morning, my half-asleep brain conjuring a fantasy timeline in which everything goes perfectly and I am not late.

My partner does not use the snooze button. My partner's alarm goes off once, and my partner simply rises, like a normal, functioning member of society, with no negotiation, no drama, no internal civil war. I watch this happen, from my own side of the bed, through one barely-open eye, with the bewildered awe of a person observing a magic trick. It is the single most impressive thing my partner does, and my partner does not even know it is impressive.

I once snoozed so many times that the alarm, exhausted, simply gave up. Most alarms stop ringing after a certain number of snoozes, a fact I discovered the hard way, when I surfaced at last from the warm depths to a silent room, a sunlit room, a room in which the morning had quietly proceeded without me. The alarm had tried. The alarm had done all it could. The alarm, at some point in the past hour, had stopped believing in me, and honestly, I understood.

On a Saturday, with nowhere to be, I will wake naturally, refreshed, at a reasonable hour, my body cheerful and ready. On a Monday, with everything to do, the same body must be dragged from sleep across forty minutes of brutal negotiation. My body knows the difference between the days. My body has read my calendar. And my body has decided, firmly, that it will only cooperate on the days when cooperation does not matter.

I have begun setting three separate alarms, at intervals, a layered defence system, a fortress of alarms. The theory is sound. The reality is that I now simply have three opportunities to snooze instead of one, three small battles to lose, and I lose all three, in sequence, every morning, and then I lie in the wreckage of my own defence system, defeated by a war I started, against an enemy that is me.

The internet went down, and so I did what we all do, what we are all secretly trained to do: I walked to the router, looked at it directly, sternly, with disappointment, and then turned it off and on again. There is no other ritual. There is no deeper knowledge. The entire population of the modern world is held together by this one act of switching a small box off and then on, and we all perform it, and we all, somehow, believe.

The router has a set of small lights, and over the years I have come to read those lights the way ancient sailors read the stars. A steady green: all is well. A blinking amber: trouble approaches. A red light, or worse, no light at all: abandon hope. I do not understand what the lights technically mean. I have never read the manual. But I know, in my bones, when the lights are happy and when the lights have turned against me.

The wifi works perfectly in every room of the house except the one room where I actually need it, which is, of course, by some cruel law of physics, the furthest room from the router. In that room, the signal arrives faint and exhausted, having travelled too far, through too many walls, and I must hold my phone aloft, near the window, at a precise angle, like a man performing a small ritual to summon a connection from the heavens.

I phoned the internet provider, and a calm voice walked me through a series of steps. Unplug the router. Wait thirty seconds. The thirty seconds, spent in silence, holding a phone, staring at a switched-off box, felt like a small enforced meditation. Plug it back in. And then we waited together, the calm voice and I, watching the lights, hoping, two strangers united in the universal human prayer that the little box would, this time, decide to work.

The wifi network in my house has a name that I chose, years ago, in a moment of misplaced humour, and I am now stuck with it forever. Every guest who visits, every repair person, every delivery driver who needs the code, must first read that name aloud, and look at me, and I must explain the joke, which was never very good, and which has aged, frankly, into something I would rather not be associated with at all.

The router sits in the hallway, an ugly black box bristling with antennae, and I have spent considerable effort trying to hide it: behind a plant, inside a basket, in a decorative box. But every time I conceal it, the signal weakens, because the router, it seems, needs to be seen, needs to breathe, needs to stand proudly in the open like a small king. And so it remains, on display, the least attractive object in the house, ruling over us all.

Whenever the internet slows down, my household conducts a small, tense inquiry. Who is streaming? Who is downloading? Who, in this house, is using the wifi selfishly, greedily, depriving the rest of us? Accusations fly. Everyone denies everything. The router, the only true witness, says nothing. And then the speed returns, mysteriously, on its own, and the inquiry is dropped, and we all return to our screens, until next time.

I bought a small device called a 'wifi extender', which promised to carry the signal into the distant, neglected corners of my home. I plugged it in. It created a second network, with a slightly different name, and now my phone spends its entire day in an agony of indecision, drifting between the two networks, connecting to neither, caught forever in the no-man's-land between them. I have not extended my wifi. I have given my phone a personality disorder.

The router needed a software update, and so it announced, with no consultation and no regard for the timing, that it would now be unavailable for the next fifteen minutes. It chose to do this at 8 p.m., on a Sunday, in the middle of a film. We sat in the suddenly disconnected living room, a family, looking at one another, remembering, slowly, dimly, how to exist without the internet, and it was, for fifteen long minutes, genuinely unsettling.

I went to log into my router's settings to fix a problem, and the settings page demanded a username and password, a username and password that were set, presumably by me, at some point in the misty past, and which I have absolutely no memory of. The router guards its own settings from its own owner. I now cannot fix the router, because the router does not believe I am the router's owner, and frankly, after all this, I am no longer sure either.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: On my first day at the new job, I was given a laptop, a lanyard, and a tour of the building so fast and so thorough that I retained the location of precisely one thing: the toilet. I do not know where my desk is. I do not know where the kitchen is. I do not know the name of the person who gave me the tour. But I know where the toilet is, and so, for the rest of the day, the toilet became my base camp, my anchor, my one fixed point in a baffling new world.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I was introduced, on my first morning, to approximately thirty new colleagues, in a single rapid sequence of names and handshakes and roles. I retained none of it. Not one name. By lunchtime I was navigating the office through a careful system of vague nods and warm, non-specific greetings, addressing everyone as a friendly 'hey', a strategy I will now have to maintain, undetected, for the entire duration of my employment here.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: On my first day, I was determined to make a good impression, to seem capable and calm. And so, naturally, within the first hour, I managed to send a test message to the entire company instead of one person, spill coffee on the welcome pack, and confidently introduce myself to a man who, it turned out, also did not work here, and was in fact also new, and also lost, and we have, in our shared confusion, become genuine friends.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: The hardest part of the first day at a new job is lunch. There is a moment, around noon, when everyone disappears, and you do not know where they have gone, or whether you are invited, or whether there is a 'lunch culture' here, or whether you are meant to eat at your desk. I spent my first lunch sitting very still, eating a sandwich slowly, watching the office, gathering intelligence, like a small anxious spy on a deeply low-stakes mission.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I spent my entire first day in a state of intense, performed competence, nodding thoughtfully at information I did not understand, taking detailed notes on a process I could not follow, and saying 'great, makes sense' a great many times. It does not make sense. None of it makes sense. But the new job does not know that yet, and I intend to keep it that way for as long as I possibly can, ideally several months.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: They gave me a list of accounts to set up on my first day, each requiring a password, and so my new job began, as all things now begin, with the creation of eleven new passwords, all of which I have already forgotten. I have been employed here for six hours and I am already locked out of three internal systems. The new job thinks it has hired a professional. The new job has, in fact, hired a man who cannot get into his own email.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: On my first day, a friendly colleague offered to take me for a coffee and 'show me the ropes'. The ropes, it emerged, were primarily a forty-minute briefing on office politics: who to trust, who to avoid, whose stapler not to borrow, and the full, complex backstory of a feud between two departments that began, apparently, over a Christmas party in 2016. I have learned nothing about my actual job. I have learned everything about the war.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I arrived for my first day forty minutes early, out of nervous overcaution, and then had to wait outside the building, in the cold, because arriving forty minutes early is, socially, almost as strange as arriving late. I walked around the block. I looked at my phone. I bought a coffee I did not want. I have, in essence, begun my new career by loitering suspiciously near my own workplace, and I hope nobody important was watching from a window.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: By the end of my first day, I had attended three meetings, the purpose of which I did not understand, about projects I had never heard of, involving people whose roles remained a mystery to me. I sat in each one, nodding, occasionally writing a word down to seem engaged. The word I wrote most often was 'synergy', because everyone else kept saying it, and I have decided that if I say it too, eventually, with enough confidence, I will become a real employee.

subtopic: first day at a new job
sentence: I went home after my first day at the new job utterly, profoundly exhausted, despite having, by any objective measure, achieved almost nothing. I had filled in some forms. I had been shown a printer. I had eaten a sandwich anxiously. And yet I was as tired as if I had dug a trench, because the real work of a first day is not work at all, it is the relentless, full-body effort of being new, and being new is the most tiring job there is.

My umbrella, the moment the wind reached a certain modest speed, decided it no longer wished to be an umbrella and inverted itself entirely, becoming a sort of useless metal flower, a tulip of failure, blooming above my head. I struggled with it on the street corner, in the rain, fighting my own umbrella in front of a bus queue, and eventually it surrendered, broken, and I carried its corpse to the next bin, defeated and considerably wetter than if I had simply owned no umbrella at all.

I own, at any given time, either zero umbrellas or seven umbrellas, and there is no stable middle state. On a sunny day I will discover four umbrellas in my hallway and wonder where they all came from. On a rainy day, the same hallway will be, mysteriously, entirely umbrella-free, every single one of them having quietly slipped away to wherever umbrellas go, leaving me to face the weather with nothing but a newspaper and regret.

Walking down a crowded city street in the rain is a slow, perilous fencing match conducted entirely with umbrellas. Everyone holds their umbrella at a slightly different height, and so the tall person's umbrella jousts with the short person's umbrella, spokes interlock, apologies are mumbled, and the entire pavement becomes a low-speed collision of nylon domes, everyone soaked anyway, the umbrellas having achieved nothing but a kind of communal, dripping chaos.

I left my umbrella, a good umbrella, a reliable umbrella, on the train. I have done this so many times that I have begun to think of it less as losing umbrellas and more as gently donating them, one by one, to the railway network, a slow and unintentional act of charity. Somewhere there is a lost property office containing a small museum of my former umbrellas, each one a monument to a journey on which I did not, quite, remember everything.

I bought a small, compact, folding umbrella, the kind that promises to live discreetly in a bag, ready for any sudden shower. It folds beautifully. It unfolds with a satisfying flick. What it does not do is keep any meaningful portion of a human being dry. It covers, generously, my head and one shoulder. The rest of me is simply offered to the sky. It is less an umbrella and more a small polite hat I have to hold.

The moment I opened my umbrella, having stepped out into a determined drizzle, the rain stopped. Not slowed. Stopped. Entirely. The sky, which had moments earlier been weeping, simply ceased, as though it had been waiting for me to commit to the umbrella before calling the whole thing off. And so I walked the rest of the way carrying an open umbrella under a clear sky, looking like a man who had badly misjudged the situation, which I had.

There is a particular art to entering a building with a wet umbrella, an art I have never mastered. I arrive, dripping, and stand in the doorway, performing a complex and clumsy procedure: shaking the umbrella, which sprays everyone nearby, then trying to collapse it, which traps my hand, then looking, desperately, for the special umbrella stand that the building never, ever has. I end up carrying the wet umbrella around with me all day, leaving a small, sad trail.

The cheap umbrella I bought from a man on a street corner, at a moment of desperate need, during a sudden downpour, lasted exactly the length of that one journey. It got me home. And then, having fulfilled its single purpose, it fell apart entirely, the fabric parting from the frame, the handle going its own way, as though it had been built, deliberately, with a lifespan precisely calibrated to one rainstorm. I respect the engineering. I do not respect the man.

I shared my umbrella with a friend, an act of kindness, and discovered that sharing an umbrella is, in fact, an impossible geometric problem. The umbrella is sized for one. To cover two people, we must walk pressed unnaturally close together, in an awkward, shuffling lockstep, each of us subtly leaning toward the other, and even then, one shoulder of each of us remains permanently in the rain. We did not stay dry. We did, however, become much closer friends.

I have, over many years, become a connoisseur of umbrella failure, and I can now identify, by the sound alone, the precise moment an umbrella gives up. There is a small metallic click, a tiny snap, and then a section of the umbrella simply goes limp, droops, dangles, and from that moment on the umbrella tilts at a permanent jaunty angle, channelling rain directly down the back of my neck, and I know, instantly, that another one has been lost to the cause.

There is a moment at the end of every video call when six adults must say goodbye, and nobody knows how. We all wave. We all say 'bye' over the top of one another. We all reach, simultaneously, for the small red button to leave, and then someone says one final thing, and we all stop, and wave again, and the goodbye stretches on, layered and chaotic, until at last the screen goes blank and the suffering ends for another day.

I joined the video call confidently, opened my mouth to greet everyone, delivered a warm and slightly witty hello, and then noticed, from the small frozen icon, that I had been on mute the entire time. I had performed my charming greeting to no one. I now had to deliver it again, the exact same words, but this time as a tired, deflated echo of itself, the wit long gone, and everyone politely pretended the first attempt had not happened.

The video call has a strange power to make ordinary objects in my home suddenly visible and suddenly shameful. I sit there, professional, attentive, and behind me, on camera, for all my colleagues to study, is a drying rack of laundry, a houseplant that has clearly seen better days, and a single mysterious shoe. I cannot move them now. I can only sit very still, hoping nobody comments on the shoe, while internally narrating apologies for the shoe.

On a video call, the great terror is the small grid of faces, because in that grid is my own face, looking back at me, and I cannot stop watching it. I am meant to be listening to a colleague discuss the quarterly figures. Instead I am studying my own forehead, adjusting my own expression, wondering if I always look like that, slowly spiralling, while the quarterly figures wash over me, entirely unheard, lost to the bottomless distraction of my own broadcast face.

Two people on the video call began to speak at exactly the same instant, and then both stopped, and then both said 'sorry, you go', and then both started again, simultaneously, and stopped again. This polite collision repeated four times, a small loop of mutual deference, while the other twelve participants watched in silence, until finally a third person, taking pity, simply talked over both of them, breaking the spell and saving us all.

Someone on the video call has not muted their microphone, and so the entire meeting is now accompanied by a rich soundscape of their personal life: a kettle, a dog, a distant child, the unmistakable crunch of someone eating crisps directly into the void. Nobody knows who it is. Nobody will say anything. We simply continue the meeting over the top of this mystery person's afternoon, all of us pretending we cannot hear the crisps, all of us hearing the crisps.

My internet connection faltered during the video call, and so my face froze, mid-sentence, in an expression I had not chosen and would never have chosen, a strange, distorted, half-formed grimace, held aloft for all my colleagues to contemplate for a full eleven seconds. When the connection returned, nobody mentioned it. But they had seen it. The frozen face is out there now, lodged in eleven memories, and there is nothing, ever, that I can do about it.

Someone on the video call decided to use a virtual background, a serene tropical beach, to hide their actual room. But the technology was imperfect, and so throughout the meeting, parts of this colleague kept vanishing into the beach: an ear would disappear, then return, a hand would dissolve into a palm tree. They discussed a serious budget matter while flickering in and out of existence, a man slowly being consumed by a fake island, and we all just carried on.

At the end of the video call, the host said the dreaded words: 'any questions before we wrap up?'. The screen filled with silence. Twelve faces stared back, each one performing a small theatre of thoughtfulness, each one praying nobody would speak, because a question now would cost everyone another ten minutes. The silence held. We had, collectively, willed the meeting to end, and our shared, desperate quiet was, in its way, the most unified the team had ever been.

I attended a video call from my sofa, dressed, as is now traditional, in a perfectly respectable shirt and a pair of pyjama bottoms that the camera would never see. The call proceeded smoothly until I needed to fetch a document, and forgot, in the moment, the precise nature of my lower half, and stood up, and walked across the room, fully visible, my professional top and my disgraceful bottom both on display, and the meeting, I noticed, went very quiet.

The television remote has vanished, and so my entire household has now stopped what it was doing and entered a state of full archaeological excavation. Cushions are lifted. Hands are plunged into the dark crevices of the sofa. The search has spread, illogically, to the kitchen, to the bathroom, to rooms the remote has never visited. We could simply press the buttons on the television itself, but nobody will say this, because the remote must be found, on principle, and the principle is sacred.

I have searched for the missing remote for twenty minutes, and in that time I have found a single sock, two pens, a coin, an old shopping list, and a remote for a television I no longer own. I have found everything except the one thing I am looking for. The sofa, it turns out, is not a piece of furniture but a portal, a small domestic Bermuda Triangle, and the remote has gone wherever the things go, and it may never come back.

The remote was found, eventually, in the refrigerator, resting calmly between the butter and the milk, cold to the touch. Nobody admitted to putting it there. Nobody could explain it. But somebody, at some point, in a moment of profound mental absence, had carried the remote to the kitchen, opened the fridge, and set it down, and that person walks among us still, unidentified, and frankly, a little frightening.

There is a deep and unspoken law in my household that whoever holds the remote holds the power, and so the remote is never simply set down. It is guarded. It is placed deliberately, on the arm of the chair, beneath a protective hand. To leave the room while holding the remote is to surrender the throne. I have learned to take the remote with me to the kitchen, on principle, a small black sceptre, lest a sibling stage a quiet coup in my absence.

The remote has been missing for so long now that we have, as a family, simply begun to adapt. We have learned to operate the television via the small, awkward buttons on its underside, a clumsy fumbling ritual performed kneeling on the carpet. We have lowered our expectations. We watch whatever channel the television was on when the remote vanished. We have built an entire new way of life around the loss, and honestly, we are managing.

I sat down, finally, after a long day, ready to relax, and reached for the remote, and the remote was not where the remote should be. And in that small moment something inside me broke. It was not about the remote. It was about everything. The remote had become, in an instant, the symbol of all of life's small, grinding injustices, and I sat there, in the dim room, defeated by furniture, contemplating the universe.

We bought a small device, a little tag, that you attach to things so they can never be lost, and we attached it to the remote, triumphant, certain we had solved the ancient problem forever. The remote, however, is no longer lost. The little tag's own remote, the thing that finds the thing, is now lost. We have simply moved the problem one step along, and the new lost object is smaller, and harder to find, and we are, if anything, worse off than before.

My television came with not one remote but three: one for the television, one for the streaming box, and one whose purpose remains, to this day, a complete mystery to everyone in the house. To watch anything, I must locate and coordinate all three, a small orchestra of remotes, and the act of changing the channel has become a multi-stage procedure requiring the focus of an air traffic controller and the patience of a saint.

I found the remote at last, wedged deep in the gap between the sofa cushions, and pulled it free in triumph, and it was, of course, completely unresponsive, its batteries having quietly died somewhere during its long exile. And so the search for the remote, that great quest, that ordeal, was simply the prologue to a second quest, the search for two small batteries, which are also, naturally, nowhere to be found in this house.

I have noticed that the remote is only ever lost when I am comfortable. When I am standing, energetic, ready to move, the remote sits in plain sight, mocking me with its availability. But the instant I have settled deeply into the cushions, arranged a blanket, achieved the perfect cosy stillness, the remote becomes, by some cruel law, undiscoverable, just out of reach, requiring the one thing I am no longer willing to do, which is get up.
